Located below an early 20th-century house in the Mexican capital’s historic colonia, Libreria Valladolid was designed to evoke the experience of exploring old bookshops. Photo by Rene Villaseñor Photography Previous Next Photography Close “It captures the thrill felt when entering these places, searching for a unique story that has patiently waited among thousands of books on all topics and from many eras,” said Em-Estudio . Accessed from the street through an unassuming door, the entry vestibule features shelves packed with old volumes and more stacks along a wooden staircase that descends to another threshold. Photo by Rene Villaseñor Small lamps are squeezed between the spines and placed on top of the stacks, creating a moody glow that sets the scene for the bar beyond. “The old bookstore is encountered upon entering, as you descend the stairs, and it remains behind as you cross the first threshold, where the books transform into the skin that embraces the rooms,” said the studio. Inside the basement, dark herringbone flooring and surfaces drenched in burgundy continue the bookshop atmosphere. The larger walls are lined entirely with shelves filled with books stacked spine inwards, so the warm beige of their pages faces the room. The restaurant is a home base for local chef Francis Blais in the city’s hip Mile End neighbourhood. Photographs Previous Next Photographs Close Atelier Zébulon Perron took what it views as the standard design language of a Montreal bistro – bright lighting and lots of activity – and translated it into a more contemporary design. For studio founder Zebulon Perron, the monochrome whites and beiges, interspersed with milled aluminium accents and a large zinc bar top, allowed the studio to experiment with textures and lighting to create visual interest and contrast in the dining space. “With the monochromy of the restaurant, we experimented with textures – shiny versus matte, tile nd and stucco – and how light reacts to those surfaces in different ways,” Perron told Dezeen. The studio emphasised the postmodern and “retrofuturist” elements of the design, pointing to the custom chandeliers with their illuminated Pyrex tubes and exposed wiring, fabricated by Perron’s long-time collaborators, local lighting design studio Lambert & Fils . Inspired by visits to listening bars in Tokyo, the trio envisioned Echo as a flexible space that can host different events and activities, but primarily focuses on the experience of music. Located on the ground floor of Groot Handelsgebouw, a post-war office block opposite Rotterdam Centraal station, the bar has an interior designed by Cournet’s architecture and design studio, Cloud . Cournet said the idea was to adapt the concept of the listening bar to the creative energy of Rotterdam. “We wanted to make it super local,” he told Dezeen. The main bar, which functions as both a service counter and the DJ area, exemplifies this approach. Built in collaboration with Barendregt’s Kistenfabriek , a company that manufactures wooden shipping crates, together with carpenter Simon Fitskie, it’s a reminder that Rotterdam is home to Europe’s largest seaport. Its sides are printed with the words “handled with care”, which became Echo’s tagline. “We thought it would be so cool make the bar an art crate because we treated everything, from music to hospitality, as if it were art,” said Cournet. “We always wanted to do everything in the best way possible.” The space features several works by Rotterda

Simone Book Services is a Copenhagen shop specialising in rare and independent books and magazines, but it can also be an exhibition gallery, a listening space, or a venue for book launches and other informal gatherings. Turkish-born architect Arpac oversaw the intentionally “un-Scandinavian” interior, which includes modular shelves made from aluminium and cherry wood, mobile book trolleys and a counter dressed in leather. Gallery Previous Next Gallery Close The concept for the store was born out of conversations between Arpac, who works for furniture brand &Tradition , and founders Tugce Kayar Subay and Ibo Subay, a married couple with backgrounds in fashion media and marketing. The Subays had amassed such an impressive collection of art, design and fashion literature that they launched a “literary branding” business in February 2026, curating libraries for exhibitions, offices and brand spaces. Simone gives the couple a physical platform for this business and allows it to evolve further. It showcases their curation of books and magazines, but also furniture and objects related to reading culture. “Tugce is the book nerd, and I’m the design nerd; we came up with this idea of combining our passions,” Arpac told Dezeen. “We wanted to create a space where people would co

When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos’s famous bar , an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. Photography Previous Next Photography Close “The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference,” studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen. “The ambition was never to recreate Loos’s bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann’s Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project,” he explained. “Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character.” Located just across the road from the city’s popular Bar Basso , Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom. Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020. The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics. A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni. The interior of the cafe is dominated by the large Blue Lantern installation above the coffee counter. Gallery Previous Next Gallery Close “The main idea came from Thailand’s traditional lantern festival,” I IN co-founder Yohei Terui told Dezeen. “We wanted to capture the feeling of a lantern floating in the sky and bring that into the space in a contemporary way.” “This became what we call the Blue Lantern, a large sculptural element extending from the ceiling above the drip station,” he continued. As it is the brand’s first cafe in Bangkok, the studio wanted to design a “bold and dramatic” space that would also nod to local culture. “The lantern idea came from the local culture, and from the beginning, we wanted to make it as large and impactful as possible,” Terui said. “We placed it at the location where customers first enter the cafe, so it would immediately catch their attention and become a symbol of the store.” The furniture and fixtures in the 178-square-metre cafe were made from teak wood, a material that is often avoided in the West due to concerns about illegal logging , but which is local to Thailand. “Every country has their own approach to natural materials, depending on what is locally available and traditionally used,” Terui said. “In Thai

The spacious eatery is housed within a nineteenth-century gothic building, which features double-height ceilings and an expansive glass facade with intricate detailing. The design was informed by traditional Parisian bistros Located in Covent Garden, the restaurant spans 107 square metres and accommodates 52 customers across a ground floor dining room and a basement level. An outdoor terrace welcomes an additional 30 guests when the weather permits. “Our brief talked about a neighbourhood restaurant in the centre of town,” Gundry & Ducker co-founder Tyeth Gundry told Dezeen. “From there, the conversation centred on familiarity, recognition and ease – creating a neighbourhood restaurant for friends who live in different parts of the city.” The studio chose a warm, neutral colour palette for the interior The studio intended for the design to resemble traditional Parisian establishments by incorporating familiar elements, including deep aubergine finishes, dark banquette seating and classic bentwood bistro chairs. Alongside this, the designers combined natural fabrics, sapele wood and stainless steel with exposed brickwork to create a restrained colour palette and an overall “deliberately unfussy” interior. Located in the city’s Escandón I neighbourhood, Nota Tavern is a two-storey Italian-American restaurant. It sits on a site that once held a hacienda-style residence that was converted into an apartment building, with the owner preserving half of the original house. The restaurant sits in this portion. Formant Studio designed the interiors and most of the furniture at Nota Tavern in Mexico City Formant Studio was tasked with translating the design of classic Chicago taverns into a contemporary mode. “The main request was to create a faithful interpretation of the neighbourhood taverns of Chicago – the kind of places built less around spectacle and more around familiarity,” Formant Studio co-founder Alejandro Valencia told Dezeen. “The design translates the character of a classic tavern into a contemporary architectural language.” The two-storey restaurant serves Italian-American cuisine Valencia also said the studio took other cues from Chicago and integrated the clean minimalism of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and the warmer modernism of Frank Lloyd Wright , both architects known for their work in the US city. Named after Greenspan ‘s daughter Vivienne, VV’s Cocktail Room (VV’s) is located in Chelsea and contains just 18 seats to mimic the intimacy of an omakase cocktail experience, where bartenders lead a multi-course tasting or cocktail menu. Josh Greenspan and USM have completed Manhattan cocktail bar VV’s Cocktail Room The project stems from Greenspan’s ongoing conversations with USM, which frequently collaborates with designers to outfit spaces and create installations from the flexible panelling system. “I started imagining something a little wild – a space built entirely from the USM system, pushing its modularity in unexpected ways,” Greenspan told Dezeen. “I’m thrilled that the USM team embraced the idea and came along for the ride.” The space is wrapped in a dark blue USM Haller System Visitors to the bar pass a glass block wall partition to enter the space. Inside, navy blue USM panels form the walls that surround the space and wrap behind the bar, where they jut out into shelving. A dark walnut wood was used for the bar top and tables, which is offset by bar seats upholstered in a burgundy fabric and banquette seating built by Greenspan’s father, Michael Greenspan, covered in a similar hue. Located in the city’s Le Marais neighbourhood in the 4th arrondissement, Arcane 17 is a petite eatery that sits within a centuries-old building. Arcane 17 is a Basque and Catalan restaurant Bétyle Studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche wanted to honour the owners’ Catalan roots through their restaurant design. “Rather than reproducing the codes of a traditional Spanish restaurant, we wanted to reinterpret the idea of the Iberian tavern through a more contemporary and refined language,” studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche told Dezeen. Bétyle Studio designed the interiors for the space In this spirit, the designers clad the open space in an abundance of wood. The dining area is characterised by ebonised panelling, while the tubular stainless steel bar is topped with delicate slabs of marquetry detailing playful motifs, from shooting stars to a cartoonish lobster. Named Dayun Landison Manor, the hotel occupies the elongated site of a demolished village. It stretches 360-metre-long from east to west, with a maximum width of 54 metres in the middle that narrows to 21 metres at the ends. HB Architects and Nature Times Art have completed a hotel in Jiashan The hotel is formed of numerous buildings connected by a walkway raised 4.9 metres above ground. According to the studios, this horizontal layout is a nod to the history of the site and an attempt to recreate a village-like neighbourhood. “We fictionalised a village to continue the functional essence of ‘dwelling’,” HB Architects and Nature Times Art told Dezeen. Terracotta red and earthy yellow are used as the main colours of this building The raised guest rooms were also designed to reference local housing, which is often supported on pilotis. However, the columns supporting the structures were deliberately hidden to highlight the visual dominance of the horizontal slab that runs through the site. The slab is 1.1 metres thick and sits 4.9 metres above the ground The hotel’s entrance opens into a courtyard with a lake at its centre and a “water curtain” that falls from surrounding walkway. Guests then walk up stairs to the raised walkway that passes around courtyards and gardens to get to the rooms. The hotel’s spatial design was led by Kuang Ming (Ray) Chou, founder and creative director of Vermilion Zhou Design Group and chief designer of H World Group. H World debuted its Grand Ji Hotel during Paris Design Week According to H World, Grand Ji Hotel draws on the phrase “the formless greatness, a quiet way of seeing” and is informed by the Taoist concept of 大象无形, which suggests that the most powerful forms are often “quiet and insular”. Instead of an overtly luxurious look, the hotel’s aesthetic is described as “quiet, yet possessed of presence, unlayered, yet full of depth”. The technology woven into the design ensures the guest experience is seamless Rather than weaving traditional Chinese imagery throughout the hotel design, Grand Ji Hotel was designed to break the conventional hotel paradigms and instead focus on quietly enhancing visitor experience. For example, the way guests arrive, dine, rest and depart are treated as part of one integrated system. Astet Studio used the Japanese concept of Utsuroi to evolve the hotel’s lobby, bar, gym, members’ lounge and Mitsu restaurant . The 164-room hotel, originally built in 2017, is defined by its striking industrial facade, featuring cantilevered balconies framed in glass, steel, and concrete. Named the Pasona Natureverse Retreat , the hotel at the tip of Awaji Island near Kobe was designed for long-term stays based on the ideal of Mibyo – an ideal of preventive wellness treatment that translates as “pre-illness”. The hotel is the third project designed by Ban for Japanese company Pasona Group on the island. It follows a thatch-topped restaurant and a wooden meditation retreat . Shigeru Ban designed the Pasona Natureverse Retreat According to Ban, the hotel’s D-shaped form was designed to take advantage of its location between the coast and a forest. “To express the characteristics of a site defined by these two completely contrasting landscapes, distinct facades were designed for the east and west sides,” said Ban. “Two linear structures with individual qualities are integrated into a single D-shaped plan, flanking a light-filled atrium.” The hotel stands on the seafront The five-storey hotel was designed primarily for long-term, 30-day-plus retreats, as well as offering shorter stays. Its 57 rooms are arranged around a large, skylit central atrium with half overlooking the sea and half facing the forest. While the landward facade is adorned with stylised timber columns, the seaward side was designed to express horizontally, with balconies running the full width on all levels. Named Yarlington Lodge , the buildings are spread across five hectares of rural land at The Newt in Somerset , a luxury estate, hotel and working farm located just outside of Bruton. Yarlington Lodge is a three-building holiday home at The Newt in Somerset Conceived by Richard Parr Associates as a 32-guest holiday home, the project comprises the main lodge, the Coach House and the Cottage in the Wall – three buildings that historically served as a rectory, its coach house and the gardener’s cottage, respectively. “They were once a functioning trio and we wanted them to become so again,” studio founder Richard Parr told Dezeen. Patterns and bright colours reference the Napoleonic era in the main lodge The architect worked with The Newt in Somerset’s founders, Koos Bekker and Karen Roos, to restore each property. For the 1831 lodge, striking patterns and bright colours were selected to reference the high drama of the Napoleonic era . The Coach House was renovated to reflect its equestrian history Bedroom ceilings were clad with swooping textiles that give the impression of military tents, while classical paintings embellish the green-hued library. KTGY ‘s Interiors Studio was brought on to refresh the detailing and bring light into the dark spaces of the hotel, with a focus on the premium rooms and lounges. In total, the studio renovated 83 rooms, as well as meeting rooms and a terrace on the second level. KTGY has revamped the Fairmont Chicago Millennium Park hotel Originally designed by global studio HOK in the 1980s, the postmodern skyscraper hotel in Chicago’s Millennium Park neighbourhood features a rationalised structure with neoclassical columns at the base. At the top, it’s crowned by an oxidised copper turret that recalls the distinct châteauesque style of Fairmont hotels. However, the elongated body gives the building a sense of verticality more akin to a modern skyscraper, with the mix of the historical and industrial contributing to the “postmodern” descriptions of the building. The scope included lounges and premium rooms The studio said that the primary reason behind the renovation was reflecting aspects of the postmodern skyscraper’s facade in the interior, bringing the details down to scale. “KTGY’s interiors team reflected the building’s postmodern architectural style by bringing that prominence down to a human scale,” said the team. Located on Queen’s Road in Hong Kong’s Central district, the hotel was first established a decade ago. It recently reopened after the completion of interior renovation by Joyce Wang Studio and a new facade design by Neri&Hu . Terracotta tones in the lobby nod to Hong Kong’s colonial architecture Joyce Wang Studio referenced Hong Kong’s historic architecture and skyline when designing the hotel, whose interior was informed by the city’s colonial country manors. “We took inspiration from the colonial country manors frequented by the Tai Pans of a bygone era to celebrate the beauty of these historic homes that still fascinate today,” Wang, principal of her eponymous studio, told Dezeen. “Our vision this time has a greater focus on local relevance and the heritage of the building.” The studio also aimed to fuse art into the hotel . “We also used art as an integral part of our philosophy for the space, with a commitment to adding local flavour. The artwork program is rigorous in that there is a story behind each piece,” Wang added. Undulating staircase extends around a large-scale contemporary artwork The hotel lobby features a mix of materials including stone, timber and textured wallcoverings. Custom eglomisé glass was added as detailing to create a contemporary atmosphere.

A stainless steel bar sets the tone upon entry The original building dates from the 1920s and before the intervention, it was divided into two distinct units: one contained a cafe, while the other housed a bookshop. It now functions as one cohesive interior subdivided into three spaces, all of which reference retro workplaces. Occupying the basement levels of a building in Marylebone, Dive features furniture and materials that adapt to different scenarios and celebrate signs of use. Golem has designed the interiors for Marylebone bar Dive “Dive’s experience is an ongoing negotiation between the design and its guests,” explained Golem founder Ariel André. “The bar is not finished at opening, it is finished nightly, by hands, shoes, spills.” “Wear and tear is part of the architecture,” he added. “Glossy surfaces are designed to take scratches from glasses and jewellery, velvety walls and floors are meant to retain the imprint of bodies.” The bar is covered almost entirely in red velvet Dive’s owner chose to divide the venue into two distinct zones: a luminous bar area near the entrance and a darker, more intimate lounge reached by descending a short flight of steps. Clean lines and sculptural forms define the bar, which features a curved cutout along its front. Convex mirrors and surfaces rendered in smooth, glossy finishes reflect light and movement throughout the space. The fabric retains “the imprint of bodies” “The palette and shimmering light are calibrated for a transitional feel, somewhere between dusk and dawn: warm enough to flatter skin tones, restrained enough to leave the shimmering cocktails in focus,” André explained. Su Wu’s Mesoamerican Modern Made Us Rethink the Meaning of Home Casa Amalia, designed by architect Agustín Hernández for his sister, is one of the 16 homes in Mesoamerican Modern by Su Wu. Photos: Luis Garvan Admittedly I’ve only been to Mexico a few times — an Acapulco wedding, a trip to Tulum at the height of its reign, a whirlwind jaunt photographing homes for How to Live With Objects — but I don’t think I’ve ever learned as much about a place from reading an interiors book as I did with Mesoamerican Modern by Su Wu, the California-born curator and artist who moved to Mexico more than a decade ago and began inhaling the country’s customs and culture. Wu has always been a wonderful thinker; it’s what led us to her work all those years ago . Here she’s thought deeply about her adopted home and how its nuances have often been flattened or erased in our post-colonial world, but she’s also exposed how slippery a beast the very concept of home can be. The book is separated into unexpected rubrics — there’s a whole section devoted to “Unsquared Rooms” — but at its heart is a willingness, almost an imperative, to embrace different ways of living. In one section, there’s a circular house sunk into the ground, whose windows look out onto an interior courtyard; in another, there’s a house that remains forever unfinished, as its owner chips away at stone, forming sculptural reliefs. The book encourages painting everything pink, or allowing a tree to grow through the wall, or emptying a house of nearly all its furniture, leaving a bed that can be moved from room to room, depending on the season. One of our favorite projects in the book (featured in the photos above) is Casa Amalia, which the architect Agustín Hernández — widely regarded as the progenitor of contemporary Mesoamerican architecture — built in 1973 for his sister. A London Couple Asked for “Edgy and Raw.” Max Radford Delivered. We’re gagging over this London townhouse, from the teal-and-steel bathroom to the vintage paintings in the dining room to how Italian classics meld perfectly with works by up-and-comers. Photos: Michael Sinclair In one of the best interior briefs I’ve heard, the clients of this late-Victorian home in London wanted something “edgy, contemporary, and a little bit raw” — the diametric opposite, basically, of the Pinterest aesthetic. They certainly came to the right person: Max Radford , who not only runs an eponymous gallery for new talents working under pretty much the same directives, but also designs interiors as such, often incorporating pieces from his roster. Likeminded clients are every designer’s dream, but the project has me thinking with pride about how far our little world has come. It’s hard to imagine clients with-it enough to hire a decorator this way 15, or even 10, years ago. Or if they did, to give them both carte blanche and a budget (rather than either/or). Working atop an existing renovation by Atomik Architecture, Radford came through in spectacular fashion, but took care not to abuse his mandate; he added in the requisite 20th-century icons like sofas by Pierre Paulin and Alessandro Becchi, lights by the Castiglionis and Mario Botta, and a bed by Carlo Scarpa before wilding out with more directional new British talents — and that scrumptious teal-walled bathroom. The living room features a zigzag steel chair by Grace Prince, the entry hall a custom radiator cover by Radford himself, the bedroom a cabinet by EJR Barnes, and the bathroom a chair by LS Gomma as well as a mirror by Radford and Eddie Olin. A Listening Bar Where Yugoslav Modernism Meets Japanese Hi-Fi Culture Supaform’s interiors for EJE incorporate his furniture and art, plus original London Underground textiles, vintage speaker systems, and more. Photos: Varvara Toplennikova Had you visited Yugoslavia in the 1970s, you would have seen thousands of modular structures dotting the streets, instantly recognizable by their rounded, space-age exteriors and large central picture windows. Expandable to encompass anything from newspaper stands to copy shops to small cafes, these were the iconic K67 kiosks, envisioned by the Slavic architect and industrial designer Saša J. Mächtig in 1966 and now altogether more rare in the country. It was these stands — along with Yugoslav brutalism and futurism in general, plus the aesthetic and sound design of Japanese listening bars, that inspired the interiors of Esthetic Joys Embassy, or EJE , in Belgrade. Comprising a bar, a restaurant, a DJ booth, a vinyl library with listening stations, and a dance floor that’s attached to a hotel, EJE was designed by Supaform , and features not only principal Maxim Scherbakov’s furniture designs but his artworks as well, as seen in the lower right photo above. Other key details include a pair of vintage JBL 4435 studio monitors, an iconic Japanese train station clock called the Dulton Double Face, and archival Mischa Black upholstery fabric — used on the London Tube in the 1970s — that Scherbakov’s team sourced from the original London mill that made it. The idea, he says, was to transform the space into a utopia that inspired both nostalgia and optimism; “a futuristic, autonomous station of aesthetic pleasures.” One of Athens’s Great Midcentury Landmarks Enters a New Era At top, a suite at the newly renovated Conrad Athens the Ilisian; bottom, its original 1963 facade and a shot from its Yabu Pushelberg–designe

Art and Architecture Find a Perfect Dialogue Inside a Modernist Connecticut Landmark Artworks made from paper layered on top of linen canvases by Kim Bartelt, on view through tomorrow at the 1960 John Landis–designed Gores Pavilion in Connecticut. One downside of taking an annual summer break from our newsletter: We sometimes miss the window for exhibitions and other time-sensitive projects. This site-specific exhibition of new work by Berlin artist Kim Bartelt is only on view until the end of the day tomorrow, but assuming most of you aren’t anywhere near New Canaan, Connecticut, anyway, we figured we might as well enable you to enjoy it from afar. For “Exhibit No. 2,” presented by Arden + White Gallery , Bartelt installed 8 of her understated-yet-colorful paper-and-linen compositions inside the Gores Pavilion , a landmarked home designed by modernist architect — and Philip Johnson collaborator — Landis Gores in 1960. The artworks resonate with both the colors and the geometries found in the home, but they weren’t so much inspired by the architecture as chosen to complement it; if you know Bartelt’s work, you know this has been her visual language for years. As the gallery puts it: “This exhibition is not about illustrating architecture, nor about placing contemporary art within an iconic building. Rather, it reveals a shared architectural sensibility, one rooted in proportion, restraint, and the thoughtful orchestration of material, light, and space.” Walker Street Market Is Turning the Berkshires Into a Contemporary Design Destination At Walker Street Market in Lenox, Mass., the craft-forward fare includes a custom counter by Brian Persico and painting by David Silverstein (top), a side table by Simone Bodmer Turner and lamp by Ashley Joseph Martin (above left), and a teapot by Akira Satake (above right), among many others. For a Summer, the Athens-Based Gallery Antiqua is Trading White Walls for the Deep Blue Sea The Athens-based 20th-century furniture gallery Antiqua is popping up on the Greek island of Antiparos for the summer in a show called “By the Sea.” Photos: Giorgos Sfakianakis One regrettable limitation of having a permanent gallery space is that, regardless of how much exhibition design you can pull off, or how many bizarre interventions ensue, each show still retains the DNA of its enclosure. An Alex Da Corte show at Karma Gallery — even with red carpeting, pink walls, and an upside-down inflatable cat — still feels like a typical Karma Gallery show; heavy curtains or a Do Ho Suh–esque house can’t fool you into thinking you’re not at Jacqueline Sullivan’s. (Perhaps the most successful transformation of a known space I’ve ever seen was Felix Burrichter’s Charlap Hyman & Herrero–designed BLOW-UP exhibition for Friedman Benda , but that’s another story for another day about how 2019 was my favorite year in design.) This is why it’s so exciting when a shop or gallery decides to decamp entirely to a new space, whether for the long haul or even for a few months. Photography: © Galerie Patrick Seguin This week Design Miami is taking over Paris’s 7th arrondissement and with it a Jean Prouvé classic. In the garden at Hôtel de Maisons, the hôtel particulier where the fair has based itself since it launched here three years ago, the gallerist Patrick Seguin has installed one of the demountable pavilions Prouvé designed at the end of the Second World War. The 6×6 Demountable House was commissioned by the French government as a temporary, lightweight alternative for postwar homeless communities. And Prouvé, a founding member of the Union of Modern Artists with Le Corbusier , who embraced industrialisation as many designers decried it, was the perfect man to execute it. Here, the installation serves as a reminder that affordable, dignified shelter is never beyond our scope. Photography: Marco Galloway When Paul Schärer took over the Swiss manufacturer USM in the 1960s, he commissioned the influential architectect Fritz Haller to design its new headquarters. Haller responded with a flexible, modular chromed framework that could be reconfigured with ball joints to the needs of the office. He then set his mind to furnishing it, and designed a range that could match the new buildings’ sleek and adaptable structure. What he came up with was a system of steel modules that could stack vertically, laterally and elegantly. A design classic with a clean, industrial minimalism and rich powder-coated colour, the USM modular system became a mid-century classic and a staple of functional spaces everywhere. They can recede into the architecture of a space or become luxurious features when displaying collectible objects, flowers, records. But we've never seen it used in this most recent application — as the foundation for this new bar by New York entrepreneur Josh Greenspan. Photography: Marco Galloway 1 of 4 VV's Cocktail Room, named for Greenspan's daughter, Vivienne, was inspired by late nights in New York and omakases in Tokyo . Greenspan

items.text: How This New Orleans Hotel Went From Former Haunted House to Chic Destination | Architectural Digest Skip to main content AD PRO DIRECTORY APPLY NOW Architectural Digest Architectural Digest DIRECTORY ARCHITECTURE + DESIGN SHOPPING CELEBRITY AD IT YOURSELF AD PRO Menu Menu Search Menu Menu Directory Architecture + Design Shopping Chevron Celebrity AD It Yourself AD Pro Chevron Real Estate Lifestyle MORE VIDEO THE MAGAZINE NEWSLETTERS Search Search Architectural Digest Search Close Menu Menu Menu Ghost Host How a Coven of New Orleans Design Diehards Transformed This Haunted House Into a Hot Hotel An exclusive look at New Orleans’s most intriguing new design hotel, The Whit—and its scandalous, high-camp backstory By Lauren Mechling Photography by Frank Frances Styled by Sara Mathers October 30, 2026 The newest addition to the New Orleans design hotel scene, The Whit, has a history of local scandal, hauntings, and high-camp decor Frank Frances Studio Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story The Greek Revival mansion that sits at the corner of Prytania Street and Jackson Avenue in New Orleans’ Garden District wouldn’t know “dull” if it came up and rang the doorbell. The 1857 building’s first owner was a cotton merchant who died of yellow fever. Another owner was fatally struck by lightning. Fast-forward to the 21st century, when a Tina Turner impersonator bought the property and turned it into Magnolia Mansion, a B&B with suites with names like Vampire Lovers’ Lair and Moulin Rouge. A former professional boxer and local politics kingmaker took over, but things fell apart around the time of the FBI’s raid on the property. Oh, and the estate is said to be haunted . The Whit's moody mahogany-paneled library Frank Frances Studio The hotel's parlor Frank Frances Studio Named in its B&B era by USA Today as one of the top places in the nation “to sleep with a ghost” the magisterial Harris-Maginnis House earned a spot on the city’s ghost-tour circuit with an ever-mounting pile of lore. According to a spooky tour-operator website , guests at the B&B reported various eerie happenings over the years, such as the sensation of somebody tucking them in at night or a presence watching them while they slept. There were also rumblings of mysterious footsteps and slamming doors. Ghosts or no ghosts, the new team taking over the place found gothic-coded wall murals and dark purple velvet hanging at every turn. Who you gonna call to give an old haunt a new design vernacular? Gretchen Trauth, CEO of the New Orleans investment firm behind the New Orleans hotel, rang up Jensen Logan and Katie Leblanc Killen of Logan Killen, a local design firm known for infusing spaces with a beguiling mix of polish and patina. “The goal was a hotel where nobody can quite tell whether a designer has touched it,” says Logan. Whether you dream up a candy cane–inspired color scheme with elegant white china and poinsettia-red floral arrangements, or you create a winter tablescape complete with snowflakes, snowmen, and flickering tea lights, a holiday table is the perfect opportunity to get creative and channel your yuletide style. And the good news is, a holiday centerpiece isn’t just for a dining table— kitchen islands , foyers, and coffee tables all lend themselves well to a festive display. To inspire you, we’ve gathered our favorite Christmas centerpiece ideas that include everything from a classic cranberry-red palette to a designer’s chic jewel-toned Christmas table. Pinterest Photo: Lara Kimmerer 1/11 Bring the Outdoors In with a Woodland-Inspired Centerpiece If you’re going for understated elegance, take cues from this Christmas table. Layer together natural elements like foraged foliage, evergreen branches, pinecones, and antlers, then add height with candleholders. “The palette is deliberately restrained and a departure from traditional holiday decor to maintain elegance and elevate the materials,” says Rae McCalmont of PBF Homes . The Christmas decor leans into deep forest greens, warm walnut tones, soft ivory, and earthy neutrals. “Layered greenery spills organically across the table to keep the presentation soft and unfussy, metallic hints, a mix of etched and colored glassware, and eclectic dinnerware elevate the presentation, while softly glowing candlelight introduces warmth,” McCalmont says. But booking a historic hotel or Airbnb rental with a storied past —tales of tenants, centuries-old architecture, or whatever else might land a property on a local registrar—is the difference between a simple spot to snooze at night and your next dinner party conversation. From former artists’ homes and firehouses to castles and celebrity-studded hotels, we’ve curated several beguiling places around the world to lay your head at night. As is the case with older buildings, some require a bit of flexibility—say, an outdoor shower or a less-than-fully-equipped kitchen—while others offer a portal to the past (some spots on this list predate the 16th century) rich with amenities and luxury. The following historical hotels and homes have a story to tell, and guests get a front-row seat. Arrow Arrow Still Bend Schwartz House in Wisconsin Perks: Shared beach access, in-unit washer and dryer, sound system, indoor fireplace, fire pit Architect Frank Lloyd Wright built a lot of incredible spaces for others, but this is the very one he contributed to a Life Magazine article back in 1938 as part of a feature about dream homes. The four-bedroom estate is full of windows (the 63-foot living room has an entire wall of them), and each space is bursting with midcentury furniture and decor. Walking into each room feels like unlocking a new level of a time capsule, from the shag-carpeted primary bedroom to the brick-walled kitchen. While spring, summer, and fall are beautiful times to visit Wisconsin, the fire pit (and hammock) outside is still inviting come winter and snow. From $841 per night. CHECK AVAILABILITY Arrow Arrow The Scriptorium in Glasgow Perks: Badminton net, steam room, gym, BBQ grill, EV charger This is the perfect pit stop on a road trip through the Highlands. Hidden in the depths of a former abbey, this one-bedroom space used to be the “writing room” for the monastery. The bed is surrounded by stained glass windows, which look out over the gardens and Loch Ness (yes, of Nessie fame). Guests have access to the neighboring Highland Club, which houses an incredible indoor pool,

Photo: Ryan McDonald Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story As romantic as candlelight dining sounds, it’s simply not practical (way too much wax!). The best dining room lighting ideas are thoughtfully planned: They take your actual eating habits, furniture proportions, room structure, and budget into consideration. They weigh the benefits of pendant lights vs. chandeliers vs. flush mounts and wall sconces, not to mention bulb type. Lighting, it turns out, gets pretty involved—which is why we’ve tapped interior designers from around the country for their brightest ideas. And though the considerations are complex, modern lighting can be just as romantic as the candlelight option. “The evolving landscape is opening the door to more thoughtful layers and innovative ideas for how lighting can shape a space,” says Mike Shively of Chicago-based AD PRO firm En Masse Architecture and Design . “Lighting and coziness are both things we associate with luxury today, and neither necessarily comes down to price.” In fashion designer Marysia Reeves’s Venice Beach home , a breezy, lantern-like fixture hovers above the wood dining table. Photo: Ye Rin Mok Dining room lighting ideas Stagger heights Pendant lighting gets more playful when each piece hangs at a different height. The look works especially well with a vaulted ceiling, as evidenced by this dining room set in a pavilion at the back of the house. “A cluster of glass pendants hung at staggered heights works alongside a pair of table lamps on the sideboard to create warm, layered light,” says Lucas Goldbach of En Masse Architecture and Design, who worked on the project. The varying heights of the pendants gives this light fixture some dimension. items.title: In Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick’s North Carolina Home, Southern Hospitality Meets Modern Charm
items.summary: The model and tennis star recently brought their 1960s-era Charlotte home back to life without sacrificing the original appeal
items.text: In Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick’s North Carolina Home, Southern Hospitality Meets Modern Charm | Architectural Digest Skip to main content AD PRO DIRECTORY APPLY NOW Architectural Digest Architectural Digest DIRECTORY ARCHITECTURE + DESIGN SHOPPING CELEBRITY AD IT YOURSELF AD PRO Menu Menu Search Menu Menu Directory Architecture + Design Shopping Chevron Celebrity AD It Yourself AD Pro Chevron Real Estate Lifestyle MORE VIDEO THE MAGAZINE NEWSLETTERS Search Search Architectural Digest Search Close Menu Menu Menu Home Tour In Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick’s North Carolina Home, Southern Hospitality Meets Modern Charm The model and tennis star recently brought their 1960s-era Charlotte home back to life without sacrificing the original appeal By Juliet Izon Photography by Reid Rolls Styled by Sally Moore October 27, 2026 Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick with their family outside of their 1960s home in Charlotte. The interior design is by Decker, the architecture by Ruard Veltman Architecture , and the landscape design by Michelle Skiba and Autrey Kemp . The construction is by Stanwick Dunham and custom millwork by Bill Truitt Woodworks , Tyler Walker, Ellis Reid, and Blockhaus. Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story The home was, decidedly, not love at first sight for Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick . “One of the rooms had caved in; there was water pouring in through the ceiling,” Decker says of the first time the couple saw the Charlotte, North Carolina, Georgian-style house. But even in its dilapidated state, the 1960s-era home was still intriguing: It was located in the favored neighborhood for the young family, and its traditional, elegant proportions were still evident through its disrepair. At first it was Roddick, the former number-one men’s singles tennis player, who urged Decker to keep the house on their short list. Soon model and actor Decker , who grew up in nearby Matthews, warmed at the chance to rehabilitate a proper Carolina home with details like dental crown molding and classic brick. “We’d moved so many times [before this house],” she says. “And we were excited to try something new. For us, that meant a historic house with some old Southern bones.” In the entry, Roddick is seated on a vintage sofa covered in a Zak and Fox fabric. Decker stands next to the walnut staircase built by Masterpiece Staircase and finished by Tony Montognese. The custom chandelier is by Kalin Asenov, the rug is vintage, and the artwork is by Kieran Brennan Hinton. The family’s living room, clad in mahogany paneling, is Decker and Roddick’s favorite space in the whole home. The fireplace was designed by Decker, fabricated by Tyler Ernsberger, and stained by Tony Montognese, with animal carvings done by Stan Dunham. The 1930s coffee table is by Paul László, and the light fixture is a vintage Longobard for Poliarte. items.summary: Cleverly bridging the old and new with playful design schemes, amenities, and beyond
items.text: 11 Best Edinburgh Hotels for High-End Hospitality (2026) | Architectural Digest Skip to main content AD PRO DIRECTORY APPLY NOW Architectural Digest Architectural Digest DIRECTORY ARCHITECTURE + DESIGN SHOPPING CELEBRITY AD IT YOURSELF AD PRO Menu Menu Search Menu Menu Directory Architecture + Design Shopping Chevron Celebrity AD It Yourself AD Pro Chevron Real Estate Lifestyle MORE VIDEO THE MAGAZINE NEWSLETTERS Search Search Architectural Digest Search Close Menu Menu Menu Travel 11 Edinburgh Hotels Where Heritage Meets High-End Hospitality Cleverly bridging the old and new with playful design schemes, amenities, and beyond By Katharine Sohn and Audrey Lee October 26, 2026 Courtesy of Gleneagles Townhouse Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Edinburgh’s hotel scene has been a slow burn. Long-standing staples have secured the Scottish capital’s place on the hospitality map, setting a tone that’s both old-world and wonderfully warm. These classic stays have always matched the Scottish capital’s more measured, thoughtful rhythm—grand yet accessible, historic but deeply hospitable. Recently, a new wave of openings and renovations has joined them, in step with Scotland’s creative pull. Chefs, makers, and artists have been moving in, opening craft bakeries, destination restaurants, and shop-meets-galleries in fast-rising neighborhoods—and the hotels, well, they’re responding. From colorful long-stay apartments to charming design boltholes and fancy grand dames , it’s easy to find an overnight stay that matches your aspirations. If you’re in town for the Fringe and Hogmanay festivals, or en route to the Highlands, we’ve curated a list of prime spots throughout Edinburgh—from the New Town, Old Town, and even over to waterside Leith—that feel just as charming as the city itself. Arrow Arrow The Balmoral Perks : Irene Forte spa, indoor lap pool , three on-site restaurants, whisky tasting experience, afternoon tea, concierge, views of Edinburgh landmarks, close proximity to Edinburgh Waverley Station The Balmoral is one of the most popular stays and landmarks in Edinburgh. Its 190-foot clock tower—famously set three minutes fast, except on New Year’s Eve—has been part of the capital city's skyline since opening as a railway hotel in the early 1900s. After a multi-million-pound restoration by the Rocco Forte group was completed in 2025, much of the property’s charm remains in classic stained glass and the grand staircase. In true Olga Polizzi style, the interiors are a layered mix: milky creams, Hebridean blues, custom Balmoral tartan, and heather hues fill the property’s suites and communal spaces. “The Balmoral does rest and relaxation like no other through comforting amenities, charming interiors, and hearty cuisine,” says shopping editor Audrey Lee . “After a long day of taking in Edinburgh’s historic sights, there was nothing I looked forward to more than the treats from turndown service and a long soak in the glossy marble tub.” Gue

Scheduled to open in 2031, the 310-key resort will be located in Bang Tao, Phuket, marking the first property under the new luxury collection brand in Asia. The newly built property will form the hospitality centrepiece of the broader Gardens of Eden development, a 33-acre integrated luxury living and wellness destination that will also feature Etro Residences and Gardens of Eden Residences. Gardens of Eden Resort Phuket, Minor Reserve Collection will comprise a 100-key hotel and 210 one-, two- and three-bedroom residences operated as part of the resort inventory. Wellness will be a defining element of the guest experience, centred around a dedicated facility spanning more than 5,000m 2 . Dining venues are planned to include an all-day dining restaurant, two speciality restaurants, an organic café and a lobby lounge. Designed by Martin Palleros of Tierra Design, the project will reflect the natural setting of Bang Tao while delivering the distinctive character, personalised service and elevated experiences that define the Minor Reserve Collection. “Thailand is home for Minor Hotels, so introducing the new Gardens of Eden Phuket, Minor Reserve Collection to the kingdom is a significant milestone for our company and our luxury brand strategy,” says Omar Romero, Chief Development & Luxury Officer, Minor Hotels. “Phuket continues to evolve as one of the world’s most compelling resort and wellness destinations, and we are pleased to partner with Amal Group of Companies to bring this exceptional project to life.” Alexander Chuvalov, CEO, Gardens of Eden, adds: “Gardens of Eden has been conceived as a destination where luxury living, wellness and nature come together in a meaningful way. As the project enters this next phase, we are delighted to partner with Minor Hotels to introduce the first Minor Reserve Collection property in Asia. items.text: Capella to open at Dubai Peninsula in 2030 - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search Capella to open at Dubai Peninsula in 2030 2 November 2026 • Projects Capella Hotel Group has announced Capella Dubai, set to open in 2030 on the Dubai Peninsula in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The 115-key hotel will include a collection of suites with private pools, culminating in a 600m 2 Capella Suite conceived as a residential-style retreat. Set along one of Jumeirah’s most desired shorelines, Capella Dubai will open within the 210-acre waterfront destination by H&H. Conceived as a first-of-its-kind, design-driven destination, the Dubai Peninsula brings together hotel brands and private residences, complemented by dining, retail, a superyacht marina, a kilometre of private beach and over two million square feet of botanical gardens. Developed by H&H and designed by Denniston , the hotel will feature five social venues from the lobby lounge and The Living Room to the signature restaurant. Above it all, the rooftop will be home to a specialty restaurant and destination bar, inviting guests to dine against the Dubai skyline. Stretching nearly 70m across the rooftop, the pool will offer a tranquil retreat above the city, alongside single and double cabanas. A family pool will also feature at beach level. Capella Wellness will offer a holistic approach to wellbeing, encompassing the Auriga Spa, a Fitness Centre and Mind Body Studio, as well as an outdoor fitness area. Inspired by the restorative rhythms of the moon, Auriga Spa will feature male and female treatment rooms, a co-ed suite and VIP suite, alongside a hammam, hydrotherapy circuit pool, two biohacking facilities and grooming services. Dedicated relaxation lounges will offer quiet spaces to pause before and after treatments. For celebrations and gatherings, Capella Dubai will offer a spacious ballroom with a pre-function lounge, complemented by two meeting rooms, a VIP Majlis and an outdoor event lawn. “As Capella grows beyond Asia Pacific into the Middle East and Europe, we are entering an important new chapter for the brand,” says Roland Fasel, President, Capella Hotel Group. “The Middle East shares our appreciation for craftsmanship, culture and exceptional service, making it a natural home for Capella. items.text: Spagnulo & Partners redesigns Milan Marriott Hotel - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search Spagnulo & Partners redesigns Milan Marriott Hotel 28 October 2026 • Projects The historic Milan Marriott Hotel has entered a new chapter following an extensive interior renovation by Spagnulo & Partners, the Milan-based architecture and interior design studio led by Federico Spagnulo, Alessandra Carbone and Andrea Spagnulo. Encompassing the hotel’s 317 guest rooms, public areas and event spaces, the project establishes a contemporary architectural language that draws on the property’s history and its longstanding relationship with the city. The project is guided by a principle of architectural continuity, expressed through a system of geometries, proportions and materials that evolves across the interiors according to their scale and function. The grid emerges as a recurring design element, first appearing in the full-height shelving that structures the public areas before becoming a graphic motif reinterpreted in handwoven rugs and textiles. As it shifts in scale and material, its precise geometry takes on a softer, more tactile expression. In the communal areas, the design creates a sequence of spaces with different degrees of openness and intimacy. Bespoke furnishings define the various areas while maintaining visual continuity, whereas the use of wood introduces a warm, tactile element that balances the rigour of the geometry. The predominantly neutral colour palette is punctuated by carefully chosen colour accents, provided by upholstered furniture and rugs, which help to characterise the spaces and create different atmospheres. The same attention to proportion and the guest experience informs the renovation of the 317 guest rooms, where clean lines, natural finishes and contemporary furnishings create interiors conceived around comfort and functionality. The design responds to the requirements of international hospitality, balancing practical considerations with material quality and a distinctive visual identity. From the organisation of the spaces to the design of the furnishings and the lighting scheme, the project embodies Spagnulo & Partners’ bespoke approach, rooted in the relationship between architecture, materials and the quality of living. Marking the first Outset Collection hotel in Europe, the hotel features interiors by Madrid-born designer Lorenzo Castillo, complemented by views across the city’s rooftops. Casa Verbena Madrid takes its name from the traditional Spanish verbena: a lively neighbourhood celebration that brings people together through food, music and shared traditions. The hotel also draws on costumbrismo, the Spanish artistic tradition of depicting local customs, characters and daily rituals, looking beyond the capital’s landmarks to the cafés, streets and squares that shape life for Madrileños. The hotel’s interiors reflect a distinctly local perspective on the city. Costumbrismo-inspired artwork, warm materials, fluted glass, brass finishes and layered textures reference Madrid’s architectural and cultural heritage in a contemporary way. Many guestrooms look onto Preciados street and its typical Madrid façades, while Preciados Rooms open onto terraces with views across the city’s rooftops and towards the Royal Palace. “Casa Verbena Madrid offers a fresh perspective on the capital, whether guests are discovering it for the first time or returning to experience it differently,” says Álvaro Mazaheri, Managing Director, Arte Hoteles. “From a breakfast inspired by local favourites to recommendations we would share with friends, we want each stay to reveal more of the Madrid that lies beyond its best-known sights.” Elizabeth Scruggs, Brand Leader, Outset Collection by Hilton, also comments: “Casa Verbena Madrid represents the essence of Outset Collection, offering guests a stay that feels deeply connected to the destination. As our first hotel in Europe, it sets the tone for how we envision the collection growing around the world: through independent hotels with compelling stories, strong local identities and a genuine sense of discovery. With more than 100 hotels under development globally, we are building a collection of individual hotels that invite travellers to experience a destination through a more personal lens, all with the benefits of Hilton.” David Kelly, senior vice president, Continental Europe, Hilton, concludes: “Madrid is a special destination for Hilton, and in recent years we’ve broadened our presence in the city with distinctive brands and properties designed to meet different traveller needs. items.text: First Look: Andaz Turks & Caicos - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search First Look: Andaz Turks & Caicos 23 October 2026 • Projects Andaz has unveiled a first look at the interiors for Andaz Turks & Caicos. Set to open in Spring 2027, the property will mark the first Hyatt hotel in Turks & Caicos and the first Caribbean island resort for the Andaz brand. The 132-key resort is designed by architecture by RAD Architecture with interiors by Modus Operandi in collaboration with Hyatt. Gently curving with the coastline, the west-facing property will offer a sunset perspective at every touchpoint. Set directly on the white sands of Grace Bay and steps from Bight Reef within Princess Alexandra National Park, Andaz Turks & Caicos will comprise 59 hotel rooms and 73 branded residences, also available for stays, with 10 penthouses featuring their very own rooftop plunge pools. The resort will feature three swimming pools, the 7,000ft 2 Runa Spa & Wellness, four dining concepts, a dedicated Kids Club, tennis and pickleball courts, in addition to ample weddings and event space. The structural narrative of Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay will unfold around an arrival sequence that takes cues from the island’s early history, when visitors arrived exclusively by boat. The entrance will recreate this experience, translating the pier into a long, immersive progression toward Grace Bay. Guests will move along a wood-lined corridor whose framing references the skeleton of an overturned boat. Set 15ft above the sea, the vantage point will immediately give the feeling of floating over the water as panoramic ocean views open up. That connection will continue throughout the interiors, where local stone and rich, natural materials add warmth while shifting hues of blues draw the surrounding waters indoors. The guestrooms’ expansive views and indoor-outdoor living will be balanced by a sense of privacy. Teak and hardwoods, richly textured fabrics and streams of natural light filtering into the bathrooms will create a tactile warmth, while artwork by Caribbean artists and pops of colour will bring the island’s character indoors. A traditional Turks & Caicos dress, distinguished by its colourful stripes representing the individual islands, will serve as a cultural touchpoint for the interiors. The striped pattern is reinterpreted in the wooden headboards, translating a recognisable element of local dress into a subtle design detail. In addition to 59 standard guestrooms, the 73 branded residences include studios as well as one-, two-, three- and four-bedroom layouts, with the largest four-bedroom residences spanning up to 8,336ft 2 of indoor and outdoor space. Each residence will offer a balcony or terrace, indoor-outdoor living spaces and a Bosch-equipped kitchen. items.text: Rodolphe Parente envisions Experimental Roma - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search Rodolphe Parente envisions Experimental Roma 22 October 2026 • Projects Experimental has announced the opening of its new Roman address, a vibrant and cinematic hotel designed to embody a contemporary Dolce Vita. Located on the Via Veneto in a building that formerly housed a bank, the hotel features 82 rooms, a rooftop, a suspended swimming pool, and an interior scheme by Rodolphe Parente. “For Experimental Roma, I did not want to recreate or imitate a nostalgic vision of Rome,” says Parente. “Instead, I wanted to create a living tribute, a free interpretation expressed through materials and space. A place charged with the same tensions that define Rome itself: sacred and profane, splendour and decadence.” In the lobby, the designer has curated an intimate interior that blends heritage and reinvention. Italian opulence is revisited through a French lens and the legacies of great Italian masters – such as Gio Ponti, Carlo Scarpa and Luigi Caccia Dominioni – are referenced through subtle nods to the 1970s: chrome tubing, disco-inspired accents, lurex carpets, a sculptural staircase and rich and textured materials. Throughout the restaurant and public spaces, enveloping banquettes, quilted drapery and exposed beams pay homage to Italian cinema, while the rooftop features an expansive bar overlooking the Eternal City, a swimming pool and a terrace. The hotel’s 82 rooms are divided into two principal categories. The first evokes the theatrical Roman bedroom, bathed in light filtered through interior shutters. Large blocks of colour, dramatic headboards inspired by antique drapery and a sense of romantic intimacy reminiscent of Villa Medici define these spaces. Colourful basins, vibrant details and a richer, more expressive design language create a dialogue between ancient Roman baroque influences and the hedonism of the 1970s. The second category embraces a more refined, almost futuristic aesthetic. Mineral patinas, two-tone lacquered ceilings and ribbed stainless-steel headboards resembling contemporary sculptures create a contemplative atmosphere. Artworks throughout the rooms evoke the worlds of Cy Twombly, Christo, Ugo Ferranti and the Yvon Lambert Gallery. The bathrooms are conceived as contrasting boxes, balancing warm wood with cool stone, raw materials with bespoke graphic details. “Experimental Roma is a hotel of inverted perspectives,” Parente concludes. “A French interpretation of Italy; an Italy reinvented through materials, textures and light. Noble materials interact with reimagined industrial elements. Marble converses with folded stainless steel, while terracotta tones vibrate against polished metal surfaces. items.text: The Romeo Collection announces expansion to Massa Lubrense - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search The Romeo Collection announces expansion to Massa Lubrense 21 October 2026 • Projects The Romeo Collection has announced its third hotel, Romeo Massa Lubrense, which is set to debut in May 2027. The new destination emerges as an exclusive retreat suspended between architecture and nature. Designed by architect Kengo Kuma, Romeo Massa Lubrense establishes an escape centred around reclaimed time, privacy and deep connection to place. Tucked away in a secluded natural reserve in Punta San Lorenzo, the closest point of the coastline to Capri, Romeo Massa Lubrense is built directly onto a private natural fjord. Reimagined from the historic 1963 Hotel Delfino with a rigorous commitment to environmental restoration, Kuma maximises the property’s connection to its surroundings, creating a contemporary sanctuary that blends architecture and nature. The design is rooted in Kuma’s philosophy of dissolving architecture into the landscape and the Japanese concept of Ma (間), that emptiness is not absence but a silent presence. The design palette relies on warm, organic tones and natural Mediterranean materials, including local tuff, travertine, American walnut and matte ceramics. These materials, paired with transparency and the soft curves Kuma is known for, ensure the architecture achieves a sense of ‘visual subtraction’, relieved of clutter. The boundaries of the 63 rooms and suites dissolve entirely with true indoor-outdoor living, with the view over the Gulf blurring the separation between infinity pool and sea, and a minimalistic design bound by the natural surroundings that ensures the property becomes one with the sea, light, and nature that define the cliffside. “Our vision for The Romeo Collection has always been to create experiences driven by their destinations, and Massa Lubrense captures the authentic, slow-living spirit of the Italian coast like nowhere else,” says Alfredo Romeo, founder of The Romeo Collection. “I am thrilled to soon share this project, which will marry a rare, dramatic natural landscape with unparalleled design and hospitality. We are creating an ultra-exclusive retreat that I believe will truly redefine the luxury resort experience in Italy.” italy Kengo Kuma new hotel Romeo Collection The Romeo Collection Related Posts 22 August 2025 Radisson Collection debuts in Hungary 24 April 2023 The Romeo Collection expanding Italian portfolio 3 March 2014 Starwood announces five new projects in China Sign up for Sleeper's free email alerts Home About Media Pack AHEAD Subscribe Contact Cookie Policy © 2026 Sleeper Media Ltd. items.text: Paragon Studio to debut In-Suite collection at HIX Europe 2026 - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search Paragon Studio to debut In-Suite collection at HIX Europe 2026 20 October 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle Paragon Studio is taking hotel fitness out of the basement with In-Suite, a range of fitness equipment designed for guestroom-based workouts. Making its debut at HIX Europe 2026 at Stand C30, In-Suite will officially launch as the global wellness economy reaches a record $6.8 trillion, with wellness tourism alone valued at $894 billion, according to the Global Wellness Institute. The range, targeting luxury hotels who invest consciously in wellness, combines three elements: the kit, the content and the service. Each is designed to work with the others, so the room adapts to the guest’s habits and not the other way round. For hotels, it offers a wellness proposition that sits inside the suite itself, without the need for additional square footage elsewhere on the property. Research for In-Suite has been developed with the modern traveller in mind, someone who doesn’t want to use the gym but still values exercise, movement and routine. This guest profile is more likely to enjoy practicing mindful movement, such as yoga, Pilates and light mobility. The collection comprises movement, recovery and strength kits, housed in a foam insert cut to fit the room’s existing drawers, in a wooden tray, or delivered to order. Each kit carries a laser-etched QR plaque linking guests to a video library of strength, Pilates and recovery sessions, which can be branded, subtitled and filmed on site in the hotel’s own rooms. Because the inserts use joinery already in place, they can be retrofitted into rooms that are open and trading. What’s more, every piece has its own cut-out, so housekeeping can see if anything is missing. Paragon Studio will launch with three core options: the Movement Kit, the Recovery Kit and the Lite Kit. The Movement Kit includes hand-weights, a kettlebell, resistance bands and a cork yoga mat and block, all housed within a bespoke insert, while the Recovery Kit includes a massage gun, massage ball, red LED light therapy panel and a roller. Additionally, a Lite Kit, featuring a pared-back selection of equipment and select content library, is available to hotel operators seeking a comprehensive wellness offering across all room categories. At HIX Europe, the collection will be shown as a separate tray and in a bed created in partnership with Naturalmat, its drawer built into the base. The pieces will demonstrate how far In-Suite can be tailored: inserts can be cut to fit furniture already in the room, or designed into new pieces from the outset to any specification a project calls for. Throughout the two-day show, Paragon Studio’s stand will double as a recording studio, with industry podcasts recorded live in conversation with designers, operators and developers on how wellness works

Across eleven conversations filmed in Paris , the series steps away from grand, speculative urban visions to examine grounded propositions embedded in contemporary practice: shifting relationships with natural ecosystems, adaptable living structures, regional material cultures, and altered dynamics between architects, clients, and users. The first article – A World that Starts with Place – brings together two podcast conversations moderated by Iñaki Laguardia, designboom’s Managing Editor. Both episodes examine an architecture that begins by listening rather than imposing: one expanding how buildings coexist with natural elements, and the other uncovering spatial, cultural, and technological intelligence already present on site. ARCHITECTURE COEXISTING WITH NATURE AND SENSORY LIVING The first episode of the Room for Utopias podcast convenes four practitioners – Anushri Patel of HPAD, Shilpi Sonar of Creations & Urban Saints, Shiny Mariaselvam of Studio Sculpt, and Ridhima Sogani of Ankit Gupta & Ridhima Sogani Architects – to re-evaluate architecture’s relationship with its environment. Rather than treating green elements as decorative infill or post-construction additions, the panel positions natural systems as active participants in spatial design. Anushri Patel of HPAD addresses how architecture interacts with raw site conditions in regions with high ambient temperatures. items.title: How Surface Materials Shape Contemporary Interiors
items.summary: Whether in residential interiors, workplaces, hospitality environments, or public spaces, the relationship between aesthetic intentions and technical performance can redefine how surfaces are used and how they perform. A material selected for its specific color, texture, or finish must remain visually coherent when applied to furniture fronts, cabinetry, countertops, and other interior elements. Yet how can architects and designers create visually distinctive and tactilely engaging interiors while preserving their original design intentions across different applications?
items.text: How Surface Materials Shape Contemporary Interiors | ArchDaily ArchDaily Articles How Surface Materials Shape Contemporary Interiors How Surface Materials Shape Contemporary Interiors In Collaboration Listen to this article 6:58 Listen to this article 6:58 Playing this article To facilitate the design of high-quality interior concepts, EGGER has expanded its portfolio of PerfectSense lacquered surfaces. Image Courtesy of EGGER Written by Agustina Iñiguez Published on November 02, 2026 Whether in residential interiors, workplaces, hospitality environments, or public spaces, the relationship between aesthetic intentions and technical performance can redefine how surfaces are used and how they perform. A material selected for its specific color, texture, or finish must remain visually coherent when applied to furniture fronts, cabinetry, countertops, and other interior elements. Yet how can architects and designers create visually distinctive and tactilely engaging interiors while preserving their original design intentions across different applications? The choice of surface materials influences the user experience in ways that extend beyond the visual appearance of a space. Each material has its own characteristics and proportions, allowing it to establish specific relationships with other architectural elements. Material compatibility, specification reliability, and maintenance requirements must also be considered to develop a cohesive design language across a range of applications. Given the frequency and nature of use, each surface material must meet specific functional requirements while retaining its original appearance and remaining consistent with the design principles that define the project. With the PerfectSense portfolio, EGGER offers architects the opportunity to realize high-quality, contemporary interior design concepts with confidence and reliability. Image Courtesy of EGGER Rather than treating each surface as an independent design decision, EGGER has developed its PerfectSense portfolio as an integrated solution that combines lacquered finishes, coordinated materials, and specification support. The system enables architects and designers to establish a unified material language while maintaining flexibility across different applications. Exploring the Relationship Between Visual Depth and Tactile Experience Material perception extends beyond what the eye can recognize. The interaction between light, texture, reflectivity, and touch contributes to the atmosphere of an interior space, influencing how surfaces convey depth, warmth, and material character. In this context, matte finishes have become an architectural resource that offers a restrained visual expression while allowing variations in texture and color to define spatial relationships. The dark coloring of F128 PA Black Ambiance Granite in shades of blue and anthracite brings an exclusive naturalness to the room. Image Courtesy of EGGER Within the Decorative Collection 26+,

Image Courtesy of Herzog & de Meuron Written by Antonia Piñeiro Published on November 02, 2026 The Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity has unveiled the masterplan for its forthcoming archives in Marin County , California. The project, designed by Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron and Bay Area-based EHDD , transforms a mid-century modern warehouse into a cultural destination, with art installation space, flexible galleries, learning and gathering spaces, a theater, and dining offerings. The large-scale adaptive reuse project is accompanied by a transformation of the gardens and grounds of the surrounding 88.5-acre site, led by Field Operations . While the Institute's Eames Archives will form one part of the museum, its exhibitions and programming are intended to extend far beyond the work of Charles and Ray Eames , bringing together different disciplines, creative processes, and ideas. + 3 The Eames Archives project, 2026. Image Courtesy of Herzog & de Meuron In August 2025, the Eames Institute acquired the roadside campus in Novato, California, on the 60th anniversary of its completion. The industrial building, known for its folded, origami-like white hyperbolic paraboloid concrete roof, was designed in the 1960s by Polish-born American architect Jan Lubicz-Nycz for the office of modernist architect John Savage Bolles. It was commissioned by the McGraw-Hill publishing company as a textbook publishing, warehouse, and distribution facility. The company left the facility in 1991, and the building later served as headquarters and warehouse for Birkenstock USA. Today, the project to transform the complex into a new multidisciplinary museum by 2030 is in the first phase of the review, permitting, and approval process with the City of Novato. The Eames Archives project, 2026. Image Courtesy of Herzog & de Meuron The Eames Archives project, 2026. Image Courtesy of Herzog & de Meuron With an emphasis on showing process and ideas, the Institute is collecting works ranging from industrial design and painting to monumental works of art and public sculpture, to be housed in the converted warehouse. Herzog & de Meuron 's project preserves the hyperbolic paraboloid roof while integrating new building systems. The former industrial building will open to the landscape with new recessed glass facades and porches along its north and south sides. Travelers seek lounges as an escape from the anxiety, noise, and commotion of the concourse. Traditionally, airport lounges catered to this desire by emphasizing exclusivity: sleek, business-oriented safe havens that prioritized the needs of a privileged swath of travelers. Alaska Airlines sought to transform the lounge typology by providing a warm, welcoming space where all guests could find refuge – to relax, work, refuel and connect – a home-away-from-home with a sense of place deeply rooted in the Pacific Northwest. The architectural and interior design, led by Milan-based Droulers Architecture, draws on the heritage of the great historic villas of Lake Como while embracing a distinctly modern language. A soft, luminous palette of creams, pale blues and natural woods reflects the colours of the water, sky and surrounding vegetation, while natural materials and carefully selected vintage pieces add warmth and character. The result is a sequence of elegant, liveable interiors that feel both curated and welcoming. Regimen from Dedar| Image credit: Paola Pansini Design details from Dedar Young Nureyev in col. 022: A sumptuous yet understated fire-retardant velvet: a mingling of beauty, softness and colour. Soft and thick, this fabric has a deep, tidy and compact pile which underlines its personality. A discreet luminosity recalls the refinement of a precious cotton interpreted in a wide colour palette. Suitable for curtains and intensive upholstery. Lilaz in col. 003: On a textural and irregular panama weave, an artisanal flock comes to rest, depicting hills and cascades, Japanese clouds, or a landscape in Indian ink: a fluctuating picture that awakens various sensitivities. The artisanal screen-printing process harmonizes contrasts: the compact hand hosts a velvety hand-feel, and the slightly textural ground of Minima Mirabilia vibrates with delicate shades and discreet metallic accents. Set within a reimagined iconic landmark on Via delle Botteghe Oscure, the hotel is steps from Piazza Venezia and within walking distance of the Roman Forum, Pantheon and Colosseum, pairing its historic setting with a contemporary approach to art, design and dining. Image credit: Thompson Rome Thompson Rome draws on the architectural character of its 1940s home and the layered history of Via delle Botteghe Oscure, one of Rome’s most significant streets and a landmark in post-war Italian political history. Original elements, including a sweeping marble staircase, have been carefully restored, while a sculptural wall and inlaid floor by celebrated Italian artist Gio Pomodoro, rediscovered during the renovation after decades hidden from view—have been preserved and given new prominence within the hotel. Bespoke furnishings, refined detailing and layered natural materials bring a contemporary expression to the building’s history. “Rome has such a strong identity, so we wanted Thompson Rome to start with the city itself,” said Amar Lalvani, Chief Creative Officer, Hyatt Corporation and President & Creative Director, The Lifestyle Group, Hyatt. “The building, the neighborhood, the food, the people and the way Romans live all shaped the hotel. The goal was to create a Thompson hotel that feels at home in Rome, a hotel travelers want to discover and Romans want to come back to. Image credit: Thompson Rome “Rome reveals itself over time, through its neighborhoods, its art and, most importantly, its people. Mereshi was built from them. Roughly 95 percent of its materials, furnishings and equipment, from canvas and timber to FF&E, were sourced and produced in Tanzania , and more than 150 Tanzanians worked on the build. Image credit: Autograph Collection It’s the latest from Delaware Investments, following Mapito Safari Camp, and once again Dunia Design is behind the look . Taking its cue from the acacia tree, the architecture blends timber, canvas and woven details, with the layout shaped around the site’s natural features to keep ground disturbance and vegetation removal to a minimum. Eighteen elevated suites are spread across 55 acres of open savannah. Each measures 95 square metres, 50 indoors and 45 given over to outdoor living, and faces east to catch the first light. Inside, dark greenwood furniture, open shelving and locally sourced textiles set a grounded, tactile tone. Mesh panels frame views of the plains, while private decks are made for early coffee or lantern-lit dinners beneath the stars. Image credit: Autograph Collection The purpose runs as deep as the design. The camp expects to create around 100 permanent jobs, more than 90 percent of them held by Tanzanians, and at least five young women will live and train on site through a hospitality mentorship developed by the Give a Future Foundation with Hope for Girls and Women. Days begin with game drives and end with sundowners, fireside storytelling and Tanzanian music.
