Created by THG Paris in partnership with Haviland, the Limoges porcelain manufacturer, the collection introduces porcelain into decorative bathroom fittings, where it sits alongside metal as a fully integrated part of the design. THG Paris was founded in 1956 and designs and manufactures bathroom fittings and accessories in France. The brand works with architects, interior designers and project teams on high-end residential, hospitality and yachting projects around the world. Its experience in bespoke development allows it to adapt its fittings to the character and requirements of each project. Image credit: THG Paris Porcelain beyond the table Nihal was designed by the French architect Xavier Cartron. Its name comes from a star in the constellation Lepus, which is associated with spring water. The collection sets up a dialogue between cultures, expressed through their characteristic tones and materials. The contrast between porcelain and metal gives the design its distinctive identity: porcelain contributes a different surface and material quality to the fitting, while metal frames the overall composition. Haviland has been internationally renowned for its tableware since 1842. The Limoges manufacturer has kept its traditional porcelain-making expertise alive while continuing to create new designs, ranging from reissues of classic decors to contemporary pieces. With Nihal, that expertise is applied in a new setting, bringing porcelain into the functional and visual language of the bathroom. The collaboration also reflects a shared desire to combine established craftsmanship with new applications. Bradley Culmer of Fitzroy of London explains how the new Oxford Doc M Pack and digital configurator aim to make inclusive washrooms as considered as the rest of the hotel… Fitzroy of London has recently launched both the Oxford Doc M Pack and a new digital configurator. What prompted these two launches, and why was now the right time to bring them to market? Bradley Culmer: We’re seeing a real shift in the way hospitality projects approach accessibility and washroom design. Accessible facilities are no longer something that should be considered separately or added at the end of a project; they need to be integrated into the wider design vision from the outset. The Oxford Doc M Pack and our new digital configurator respond to two sides of that challenge. The Oxford Pack gives designers a considered, high-quality solution that combines compliance with a premium aesthetic, while the configurator addresses the specification process itself, making it easier and more intuitive for design teams to create compliant layouts. For us, it was about removing some of the complexity around accessible washrooms while giving hospitality designers greater freedom and confidence. Image credit: Fitzroy of London Hospitality environments can be particularly demanding, with washrooms experiencing high levels of daily use. What were the key considerations when developing the Oxford Doc M Pack? BC: Durability was absolutely fundamental. Hospitality washrooms need to perform day after day, often under considerably more pressure than a typical residential environment, but that doesn’t mean designers should have to compromise on appearance. We wanted the Oxford Pack to provide a robust, practical solution while retaining the level of finish expected within contemporary hotels, restaurants and leisure environments. items.text: Hotel review: a daydream come true at Schlosshotel Fiss • Hotel Designs Subscribe News Resource Hub Hotel Suppliers Hotel Industry Network Supplier News On The Boards Hotel Reviews Spotlight On In Conversation Hotel Designs LABS SPACE Magazine DESIGN POD Guide To Hotel Design Editor’s Picks Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Newsletter Contact Us SUBSCRIBE Hotel Designs Hotel Designs News Hotel Suppliers On The Boards SPACE Magazine Events The Tech in Hospitality Summit Industry Events MEET UP London The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Hotel review: a daydream come true at Schlosshotel Fiss WORDS BY Emma Kennedy October 29, 2026 TBLA Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Hotel review: a daydream come true at Schlosshotel Fiss Swapping the typical summer holiday destinations for the heady heights of Austria’s Tyrolean mountain range, Emma Kennedy visited Schlosshotel Fiss to find out why having your head in the clouds is the wellbeing retreat we all deserve… As the relentless summer heat pressed on into autumn, I yearned for crisper climes. To immerse myself in nature and breathe air I could feel. I dreamt of mountains and lakes, cold streams and woodsmoke. As daydreams go, I kept it simple. Had I delved a little deeper, I might have added a hotel with spas and pools, interiors that echoed the beauty outside, and a Michelin-starred restaurant – just for fun. Welcome to Schlosshotel Fiss . Image credit: Schlosshotel Fiss An hour’s drive from Innsbruck, the hotel sits high up in the Tyrolean mountain village of Fiss – quite literally looking down on all but one of its neighbours. A far cry from the hunting lodge and guest house it once was, it has been sensitively and imaginatively transformed since the Domenig family acquired it in 1991, growing in both size and scope. Still independently owned and family-run, Schlosshotel Fiss (SHF) is now led by Simone Domenig and holds the distinction of being the village’s first and only five-star hotel. Though not always a natural pairing, the luxurious 135-room, ski-in, ski-out hotel caters to families and couples alike. The result? A refreshingly relaxed ambience, with a few well-behaved dogs thrown in for good measure. As the Alpine village gives way to the slopes of Serfaus-Fiss-Ladis, SHF stands bold and tall, its generous balconies spilling over with geraniums. Inside, a vast marble pedestal table, laden with candles and flowers, holds court. A contemporary mix of seating and lighting sits comfortably with the more traditional Alpine touches, not least the staff, all decked in an array of regional Austrian attire – a quick reminder, should you need one, of just where you are. items.text: Six Million Bricks: Inside The Cape Town EDITION Subscribe News Resource Hub Hotel Suppliers Hotel Industry Network Supplier News On The Boards Hotel Reviews Spotlight On In Conversation Hotel Designs LABS SPACE Magazine DESIGN POD Guide To Hotel Design Editor’s Picks Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Newsletter Contact Us SUBSCRIBE Hotel Designs Hotel Designs News Hotel Suppliers On The Boards SPACE Magazine Events The Tech in Hospitality Summit Industry Events MEET UP London The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Where Cape Town’s working harbour meets Neri&Hu’s minimalist vision WORDS BY Sienna Shipton October 29, 2026 TBLA Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Where Cape Town’s working harbour meets Neri&Hu’s minimalist vision EDITION makes its African debut at Quay 7 on the V&A Waterfront, where Neri&Hu’s hand-laid brick hotel draws on Cape Town’s working harbour, with a soaring open-air Drum at its heart and a collection of African art throughout… Framed by Table Mountain and the Atlantic Ocean, Cape Town is defined by the interplay of nature and urban life , heritage and artistic spirit, and local identity and global influence. EDITION marks its African debut with The Cape Town EDITION – a gathering place poised to become a social nexus and a gateway to discover the city. Cape Town joins EDITION’s global portfolio of hotels in some of the world’s most sought-after destinations ranging from Lake Como and Tokyo to London, New York, Riviera Maya and beyond, where thoughtful design, carefully curated culinary experiences and a strong sense of cultural relevance come together in a way that is distinctly EDITION. Image credit: Marriott International “Cape Town has a distinctive energy shaped by extraordinary landscapes, diverse influences and an exceptional culinary scene,” said George Fleck, Senior Vice President and Global Brand Leader, EDITION. “As one of the world’s most compelling cultural capitals, it is a natural home for EDITION. This opening marks an important milestone for the brand as we continue to grow in destinations that sit at the intersection of culture, creativity and global influence.” Opening at Quay 7 on the V&A Waterfront, The Cape Town EDITION occupies a coveted position within Cape Town’s historic working harbour, a gateway that has connected cultures for centuries. The scheme forms part of the wider masterplan to regenerate the area and will help unlock affordable housing, now being progressed by the council, alongside a new canal-side public square designed to bring people together. The proposals centre on a 580-bed facility spanning student, hotel, and extended-stay accommodation, helping to ease pressure on Edinburgh’s housing stock from student and visitor demand. The development will also deliver a fixed co-working area for up to 300 people, and flexible space for thousands more, in response to the acute shortage of high-quality city-centre offices, alongside a line-up of vibrant social spaces – a restaurant, café, rooftop bar, clubhouse, theatre, and a state-of-the-art gym – all designed to spark connection and creativity. Image credit: The Social Hub Once operational, The Social Hub is expected to create up to 100 jobs, support more than 280 roles, and boost Edinburgh’s economy by £15.5 million. Research from RealWorth has shown that the group’s facilities generate at least five-times the economic and social value of standard hotels – rising to more than eight-times in Rome – by supercharging local connections, enhancing community wellbeing, and fuelling learning and entrepreneurship. The building is also expected to achieve BREEAM Excellent, underlining its high environmental sustainability standards. The work spans the ground and first floors, from the entrance, lobby and F&B spaces to the banqueting rooms and an extension to Taj The Chambers private members’ club. Having previously designed Taj The Trees in Mumbai, alongside Taj The Chambers and TH@51 at St. James’ Court in 2021, Conran and Partners has developed a long standing relationship with Taj Hotels across different markets. Image credit: Felix Speller The design takes inspiration from the surrounding historic streets and the hotel’s own courtyard. As guests move through the ground floor, the palette shifts from the light, desaturated tones of the entrance towards the deeper greens of the courtyard. The slate flooring follows the same transition, moving away from light grey to deep green as it runs through the public areas, connecting the spaces and creating a visual distinction between the different areas. The hotel occupies three interconnected Victorian buildings, with differing floor levels and existing structural constraints that presented a complex architectural challenge. Conran and Partners brought its architectural and interior design teams together from concept through to delivery, rethinking the layout to make better use of the existing footprint and improve how guests move through the hotel. A new lift was introduced, step-free access was enhanced and new openings created connections between spaces that had previously felt separate. WeWantMore rethought the lobby and breakfast area as a more social environment designed around the way guests want to use a hotel today: to meet, work, eat, socialise and spend time. Image credit: WeWantMore / ibis Antwerp Centrum Movement Within Structure Inspired by Antwerp’s music and theatre scene, the concept brings a sense of movement into the hotel. The structured language of ibis Plaza is balanced with flowing forms and softer details, creating a space that feels both grounded and expressive. At the centre is a suspended ceiling installation of sweeping felt forms inspired by birds in motion. Their curved, layered shapes draw the eye through the lobby, while changing light and perspectives give the installation a sense of movement against the exposed ceiling. Image credit: WeWantMore / ibis Antwerp Centrum Reworking the Experience The design starts with a simple shift in how the lobby is used: rather than serving a single purpose, it needs to adapt throughout the day. The layout was opened up to bring the different functions of the ground floor together. The existing meeting room was removed to expand the breakfast area, while the kitchen was enlarged and a new meeting room introduced behind the rounded bar, overlooking the courtyard. Reception and the bar now form a central social hub, while the co-working area can connect with the meeting room when needed. Curtains allow the spaces to open up or close off throughout the day, adding flexibility with a theatrical touch. items.title: Beyond the expected: exploring the creative potential of glass in hotel bathrooms

 Sienna Shipton .
items.text: Glass in hotel bathrooms Subscribe News Resource Hub Hotel Suppliers Hotel Industry Network Supplier News On The Boards Hotel Reviews Spotlight On In Conversation Hotel Designs LABS SPACE Magazine DESIGN POD Guide To Hotel Design Editor’s Picks Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Newsletter Contact Us SUBSCRIBE Hotel Designs Hotel Designs News Hotel Suppliers On The Boards SPACE Magazine Events The Tech in Hospitality Summit Industry Events MEET UP London The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Beyond the expected: exploring the creative potential of glass in hotel bathrooms WORDS BY Sienna Shipton October 27, 2026 TBLA Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Beyond the expected: exploring the creative potential of glass in hotel bathrooms Glass is proving to be one of hospitality design’s most versatile materials – Majestic London considers how craftsmanship and unexpected details can set a hotel bathroom apart… As hospitality interiors explore new expressions of luxury , Majestic London considers how texture, craftsmanship and unexpected details can bring individuality to hotel bathroom design. Quiet luxury has had a significant influence on hotel design in recent years. Muted colour palettes, natural stone, subtle metallic finishes and understated detailing have created some beautifully considered hospitality interiors. While this refined aesthetic continues to have its place, there’s a growing appetite for greater individuality. From richly layered interiors to subtle architectural details, designers are exploring new ways to express a hotel’s personality and create spaces that guests will remember. The bathroom presents a particularly interesting opportunity. It’s a space where materials, craftsmanship and thoughtful design can come together in unexpected ways. And one of the most versatile materials to work with is glass. Looking beyond the obvious Glass has long been central to contemporary bathroom design. Frameless enclosures, discreet fittings and expansive panels have helped create beautifully open spaces, allowing the surrounding architecture and materials to take centre stage. But glass also offers enormous creative potential beyond transparency. At Majestic London, we’ve always been fascinated by what can be achieved when designers are given the freedom to explore the material in different ways. A sweeping curve can introduce softness to a contemporary bathroom, complement the architectural details of a heritage property or create a distinctive feature within a larger suite. It can also offer creative solutions for more unusual layouts, allowing the shower to work naturally with the space. Decorative glass opens another world of possibilities. Eater.com Subscribe to Kangtown Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube RSS Eater Eater logo The Team Behind Soothr and Sappe Is Going Big on Vietnamese Food NYC Restaurant News The Team Behind Soothr and Sappe Is Going Big on Vietnamese Food Annam Tân will open in Midtown early next year by Nadia Chaudhury Oct 30, 2026, 2:35 PM UTC Facebook Link Annam Tân Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. The team behind hit NYC Thai restaurants Soothr and Sappe is turning their attention to a different Southeast Asian country: Vietnam. Parent company Sawasdee Hospitality Management is opening a new Vietnamese restaurant, Annam Tân , in Midtown East at 33 E. 33rd Street, between Park and Madison avenues, ideally in February. The Vietnamese focus stems from executive chef and partner Joel Chidensee Watthanawongwat. He shares that his grandmothers were from northern Vietnam, spent time in Laos, and then ended up in Thailand, where he was born. “Annam Tân is an expression of that journey, celebrating Vietnamese culinary heritage and its connections to the broader Indochinese region through a contemporary New York lens,” he writes through a rep. “Annam” refers to the name of what was the French region that is now Vietnam from the 1880s into the 1940s; “Tân” comes from the Sino-Vietnamese character that means “new.” “At its heart, the restaurant is a culinary memoir of a Việt kiều,” he says, referring to the Vietnamese term for “overseas Vietnamese.” “It’s not simply about recreating the Vietnam my family left behind, but exploring the Vietnam they carried with them, and how those traditions continue to evolve across generations.” The space is 11,000 square feet, with a bar featuring a dramatic overhang, murals of flora and birds, and pops of green and yellow. Watthanawongwat writes that the team took their design cues from French Indochine. Soothr opened in the East Village in 2020, with a pan-regional look at Thai food and an emphasis on noodles. They opened Sappe in the West Village, centered on Isaan cuisine. None of it reads as shtick. Jacob Hadjigeorgis is obviously a seasoned restaurant guy, and here, the native New Yorker has done his research. Easter eggs pay homage to a type of Lone Star State watering hole, and the cocktail program alone, with its obscure ingredients and something-for- everybody menu, is worth a double take. Facebook Link Get ready for a Filipino house party when June Baby , New York’s latest cocktail bar with ube coladas and pulutan , opens in the East Village on Wednesday, October 28, at 197 Second Avenue, between East 12th and 13th streets. Co-owners and couple Roxanne Diaz Bangalan and Darwin Pornel and their partner Ben Rojo started June Baby as a pop-up in 2025 to create spaces for Filipinos, Filipino Americans, and everyone else. The bar is “based on the idea of where we exist as third culture kids and how people, regardless of the specifics of their backgrounds, can relate to the experience,” Rojo says. The name refers to the Philippines’ Independence Day. The country declared independence from Spain on June 12, 1898, but after decades of American rule, it marked the holiday on July 4, the date the U.S. recognized its sovereignty in 1946. In 1962, President Diosdado Macapagal proclaimed June 12 Philippine Independence Day, honoring the earlier declaration. “We really loved this idea of reclaiming our identities and reclaiming our history,” Bangalan says. Pornel started developing the highball in 2015; he says the drink shows off the team’s cocktail expertise and Filipino flavors. The Turon-Tado crosses a daiquiri with turon, the Filipino dessert of crispy banana rolls, and is made with caramelized banana and jackfruit. See our ethics statement. The Hailey Bieber smoothie at Erewhon in Los Angeles. Mona Holmes/Eater LA It’s looking like Erewhon is ramping up its expansion plans in NYC. The cult Los Angeles grocer is famous for things like expensive celebrity smoothie collabs with It Girls like Zara Larsson and Hailey Bieber. On Friday, October 23, Snaxshot ’s Andrea Hernández shared a sighting of a recognizable Erewhon sign on 644 Broadway, at Bleecker Street, in Noho. The address is currently the location of hip fashion brand Kith , whose CEO, Ronnie Fieg, opened Erewhon’s first East Coast location inside his new private members’ and padel club, Kith Ivy , in the West Village. Several hours after Hernández shared the sighting, the signage was covered up. Eater has reached out for more information. Erewhon’s Kith Ivy locale isn’t a full-on grocer like its LA counterparts; the small setup is a drinks-only outpost, called a “tonic bar,” which means the menu is only available in person to members of the club who pay a $45,000 initiation fee and $10,000 in annual dues. Nonmembers can also order the drinks within a one-mile radius of the Manhattan club via third-party delivery apps Postmates and Uber Eats. Color-soaked smoothies packed with collagen and adaptogens start at $18 in NYC and soar to over $26 for a luxurious vanilla matcha libation. The NY Post rumormongers that the “insane” new smoothie bar coming to the landmark Bleecker Tower — NYC’s first Erewhon that’ll be accessible to the masses — will replace the Plantshed cafe and floral shop inside the Kith women’s boutique. Caper counterclaims the Plantshed takeover news originally flagged on Reddit is fake, speaking to employees there who were mum on any details. Cafe Fiorello , NYC’s iconic Italian chophouse across from the Lincoln Center since 1974 on the Upper West Side, has a new owner. Texas mega-billionaire restaurateur (and NBA Houston Rockets owner) Tilman Fertitta, is taking over bankrupt Fireman Hospitality Group ’s three Manhattan mainstays — Trattoria dell’ Arte, Fiorello’s, and Bond 45 — as part of a newly announced $22 million purchase in conjunction with Ciao Hospitality Group, which will act as the new operator, per the New York Post , who reports it as a Landry’s acquisition. Some of the restaurants in the Fireman portfolio aren’t joining the new family, including D.C.’s recently opened Cafe Fiorello and Fiorella Italian Kitchen & Pizzeria — both closing this October as part of the deal, as Eater DC first reported. Fertitta (and his company) scooping up legacy restaurants has been a trend, with his purchase of Keens steakhouse in New York and Union Oyster House in Boston, both of which were founded in the 1800s. Fertitta’s Titanic-sized restaurant portfolio includes steakhouse chains under the Landry’s umbrella, which include Morton’s, Mastro’s, Del Frisco’s, Strip House; Mexican cafe chain Dos Caminos; and sushi bar Blue Fin. He’s also a part owner of New York’s Catch Group, which includes scene-y spots like Corner Store , the Eighty Six , Or’esh , and Cafe Charmant. He shows no signs of slowing down in the restaurant world — despite juggling his time as President Donald Trump’s appointed ambassador to Italy (and parking his superyacht in D.C.). Fireman’s group started showing wear and tear after the pandemic, and the death of its cherished founder, Shelly Fireman, last fall at the age of 93 didn’t help, the news site notes, leaving the company with nearly $10 million in secured claims. Facebook Link John Tesar famously insulted a restaurant critic then banned her — and he had once leaned into his moniker of being “the most hated chef in Dallas.” Now, the founding chef of Knife , the restaurant that reshaped the Texas city’s steakhouse culture, is in New York, running Palladino’s Steak & Seafood in Grand Central Terminal. He says the temper is behind him. “I’m really a wise, pragmatic old man now who’s been in the restaurant business for five decades,” Tesar says. He started in early September as Palladino Restaurant Group’s corporate executive chef, overseeing the Grand Central restaurant and the Dallas location that opened about six months ago. He remains based in Dallas; he travels between cities. “Wherever I’m needed is where I go,” he says. Palladino’s Bourdain referred to Tesar with the pseudonym “Jimmy Sears” in Kitchen Confidential . In Medium Raw , he said he’s “probably the single most talented cook I ever worked with,” adding that Tesar “pretty much wrote the book” on self-sabotage, D Magazine reported in 2011. Tesar calls his recent shift away from his Dallas steakhouses a business decision: “I feel my talents can be better used with someone who wants to build a brand, who has infrastructure, who has large money behind it.” Licensing ties remain – he’s still connected to the Knife brand, but not involved in the day-to-day. Palladino’s is his focus. Owner Joseph Palladino, a Bronx-born former NYPD officer, spent decades in Las Vegas and Dallas, where he founded steakhouse Nick & Sam’s . Los Angeles’s restaurants continue to face difficult headwinds, starting in 2020 with the onset of the global pandemic and exacerbated by the Hollywood labor strikes in 2023 , which led to an industry-wide slowdown that continued into 2026. From the lingering effects of the Hollywood strikes to rising costs (labor, rent, ingredients, etc.), many factors continue to strain restaurant owners operating on razor-thin margins. Los Angeles restaurants also continue to struggle with the impact of the 2025 fires , including slow business and devastating property loss, as well as the ongoing effects of ICE enforcement. Juliet — Culver City’s Parisian brasserie and California chic restaurant from the Norah (R.I.P.) and Margot team closed in September. Juliet operated breakfast, lunch, and dinner in 2023. Though it’s been shuttered for over a month, the owner posted on Instagram that the popular restaurant might return. Shiku — Shiku , the modern Korean restaurant from Baroo’s Kwang Uh and Mina Park, closed on September 30. The Grand Central Market stand was initially slated to debut in April 2020 but was delayed by the pandemic until January 2021. Stan Lee Mona Holmes is an editor at Eater Southern California/Southwest, a regular contributor at KCRW radio, and a 2022 James Beard Award nominee. When friends traveling to Santa Barbara ask me for restaurant recommendations, Dom’s Taverna always tops my list. Then come the texts from the table, detailing every bite in real time. One friend simply said: “I’m in love with this place.” Chef Dom Crisp’s Basque-leaning restaurant opened in mid-2025 yet feels like it’s been there for years — a neighborhood gathering spot, cheery and constantly bustling. Adjacent to State Street’s north end, where cars are restricted, Dom’s draws locals and visitors alike with its vibes and its food. Operating in Santa Barbara has its privileges: Local farmers and fishermen provide some of the best produce and seafood on the West Coast. Crisp hails from Wren, Oregon, near the coast, where his family owns a 150-acre vineyard and farm on the western edge of the Willamette Valley. This is the chef you want preparing your grilled Pacific prawns and chilled Santa Barbara crab claws. El Niño weather patterns, already underway, will impact wildlife and especially seafood; Crisp’s lifelong expertise, long career in Los Angeles restaurants, relationships with local fishermen, and understanding of how elevated ocean temperatures and increasingly frequent storms affect fish are key here. Operating with genuine environmental awareness requires adjusting to what’s available on the fly. Crisp and his team adapt deliciously. Tuna crudo. Stan Lee What to order Though yellowfin tuna crudo is ubiquitous on California menus , it gets a real star turn here. Local fishermen make clear which part of the Channel Islands, directly off the Southern California coast, they caught the fish from, and Crisp’s team uses as much of it as possible. Shelby Moore Cathy Chaplin is a former senior editor at Eater LA, a James Beard Award–nominated journalist, and the author of Food Lovers’ Guide to Los Angeles. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app Thunderbolt is everything to everyone. For cocktailians, it’s the critically acclaimed, list-topping Historic Filipinotown stunner that dazzles with each sip. For gluten-free diners, it’s a rare place to dive into craggy fried chicken and flaky buttermilk biscuits safely. And for parents seeking some semblance of a social life, it’s the ultimate patio for watching kiddos while holding a world-class cocktail. Opened in 2019 by hospitality veteran Mike Capoferri and partner Rahul Marwah — who previously teamed up on an ambitious Denny’s in Manhattan — the bar beautifully blends science and soul. Eater.com Subscribe to Kangtown Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube RSS Eater Eater logo Fire-Grilled Mexican Seafood Is Coming to South Austin Austin Restaurant News Fire-Grilled Mexican Seafood Is Coming to South Austin The team behind Roya and Oasthouse will open Mi Vecino, a coastal restaurant focused on raw and fire-kissed dishes by Erin Russell Oct 28, 2026, 6:47 PM UTC Facebook Link Chef Amir Hajimaleki will oversee the menu, managed by Mi Vecino’s executive chef Jose Alajandro Sanchez. Sarah Natsumi Moore/Eater Erin Russell is a journalist and an Austin native, who has been writing about food for eight years. A new Mexican seafood restaurant, Mi Vecino, is opening in Circle C, courtesy of chef Amir Hajimaleki and his brother Ali Hajimaleki of Roya Hospitality Group. It’s slated to open between now and early 2027, per a release. The restaurant, Mi Vecino, will open at 5701 West Slaughter Lane, replacing another of the group’s restaurants, Keeper’s Coastal Kitchen , which closed Saturday, October 24. Mi Vecino, which means my neighbor in Spanish, will focus on Mexican seafood dishes, both raw and fire-grilled. That means offerings like shrimp enchiladas with white mole, ceviche, oysters, and fajitas served with fresh tortillas. Drinks-wise, there will be a full bar with margaritas, ranch waters, palomas, and other cocktails. Chef Hajimaleki will oversee the menu, which will be executed by chef Jose Alajandro Sanchez. The Hajimalekis’ restaurants are mostly clustered on Slaughter Lane in South Austin. Gastropub Oasthouse Kitchen + Bar , cocktail bar Daisy Lounge , and forthcoming Mi Vecino all share a building, and the group’s first restaurant , American spot District Kitchen + Cocktails , is just down the street. Mi Vecino replaces Keeper’s Coastal Kitchen, a different Roya Hospitality Group restaurant that closed in October. Jasmin Porter Photography This is not the first time Roya Hospitality Group has reimagined one of their restaurants. In Austin, which went without a major pro sports team until Austin FC’s inaugural season in 2021, college football reigns supreme. Nothing beats the roar of 100,00 at Darrell K Royal Memorial Stadium, but you can’t watch the Longhorns in person every day. Sausages and pitchers of beer near the University of Texas at Scholz Garten are hard to beat for ‘Horns games. If you’re a Green Bay Packers fan, there’s no place better than burger bar Billy’s on Burnet to wear your cheesehead. Soccer fans are in luck with games at Irish pub B.D. Riley’s in Mueller. While not listed below, many of Austin’s best breweries also host watch parties or have large screens for sports. Eater.com Subscribe to Kangtown Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube RSS Eater Eater logo Eater Bang Bang Is Headed to Austin Pop-Ups Eater Bang Bang Is Headed to Austin For one night only, Nixta Taqueria and Lao’d Bar are joining forces for a two-dinner-one-night feast by Eater Staff Aug 13, 2026, 10:55 PM UTC Facebook Link Eater’s Bang Bang dinner series is heading to Austin, bringing together two of the city’s most exciting restaurants under one roof for one night only. On August 19, Nixta Taqueria and Lao’d Bar will collaborate on a two-part, six-course dinner that gives diners a chance to explore Mexican and Laotian cooking back-to-back, through bold flavors, shared traditions, and personal storytelling. The evening will open with Chef Edgar Rico’s signature masa-driven cooking, including duck carnitas tacos and Denver steak aguachile. Chef Bob Somsith will follow with dishes inspired by the flavors of Laos, from shrimp ceviche with fried stuffed shrimp head to a fish laab tostada. And expect a delightful collaborative dessert showcasing the best of both restaurants. “I’ve always believed food is one of the best ways to tell your story,” says Bob Somsith at Lao’d Bar. “I’m excited to share the kitchen with Edgar and explore the common threads between Lao and Mexican cuisine. Different histories, different flavors, but the same belief that food has the power to bring people together.” Chef Rico from Nixta agrees. “Even though our cultures are oceans apart, they share so many of the same values: hospitality, honoring those who came before us, and creating flavor bombs that stop you in your tracks.” Tickets are selling out fast, so if you’re in Austin on August 19, get yours today . And download the Eater app to hear about more great events like this. See you at the Bang Bang. items.title: This Iconic New England Hotel Is My Favorite Place to Stay During Fall Foliage Season
items.summary: With sweeping views of the White Mountains, a heated outdoor pool, and fantastic leaf-peeping, this historic grand hotel keeps drawing me back.

By Caitlin Palumbo October 31, 2026 Courtesy Omni Hotels Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Welcome to Rebooked, Condé Nast Traveler's column where we share the properties our editors and contributors loved so much, they’ve booked them over and over (and over!) again. Travel journalists have their pick of the litter—so you know these are something special. At a glance: AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Property name: Omni Mount Washington Resort Location: Bretton Woods, New Hampshire Number of times visited: 6 Best for: Fall foliage lovers, friend groups, families with children, outdoorsy travelers looking for a historic mountain resort Why I first visited: Every fall, I make the drive from New York City to New Hampshire ’s White Mountains. It’s my favorite place to see colorful foliage, and the long drive is well worth it for the symphony of red, orange, and yellow that swathes the mountains each autumn. The winding roads, narrow mountain passes, and charming New England towns along the way make the journey feel less like a trek and more like part of the vacation. At the end of the nearly six-hour drive, in the village called Bretton Woods, awaits the grand, historic Omni Mount Washington Resort , a hotel I've been visiting since I was a kid. The grand resort sprawls across 2,600 acres, with 269 guest rooms and suites sitting in the shadow of the highest peak in the northeast, Mount Washington, which rises 6,288 feet. It's a massive white building with an eye-catching red-tiled roof, built in 1902 in the Spanish Renaissance Revival style. Set against New Hampshire’s Presidential Range , the contrast is striking—especially when the mountains are bursting with fall colors. Despite its scale and history, the property manages to feel homey and welcoming, perfect for a cold-weather escape . I still get a giddy feeling walking into its sprawling lobby, knowing that evenings by the outdoor firepits, foliage hikes, and dips in the heated outdoor pool are ahead. By Jessica Chapel October 29, 2026 Getty/Courtesy of Airbnb Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story I’ve visited Big Sky , Montana, a handful of times over the past six years, and I’m still completely smitten. This corner of the Rockies , roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. Winter ski days beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak give way to summer rafting trips and fly-fishing on the Gallatin River, while fall brings horseback rides that sprawl across open ranchlands, and spring offers hikes through wildflower-strewn meadows. The iconic Yellowstone National Park is about an hour south too, putting geysers, steaming hot springs, and roaming bison within day-tripping distance. The city itself is a quaint yet buzzy collection of restaurants, shops, and watering holes, all adding a welcome dose of small-town charm to all that wilderness. And lately, the destination’s hospitality scene has been booming , with a new wave of stylish hotels and mountain retreats bringing some fresh takes to the city’s rugged Western roots . From luxe resorts with front-row views of the towering peaks to authentic dude ranches and design-forward Airbnbs with cozy fireplaces, there’s an accommodation for every style of Big Sky getaway on the list below. By Laura Hall October 29, 2026 Rasmus Hjortshøj Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Copenhagen is a swimmer’s city. "The cure for anything is salt water: sweat, tears, or the sea," Danish author Karen Blixen, who lived up the coast from Copenhagen, famously wrote in 1934. Locals and visitors alike have taken her words to heart ever since. In the early 2000s, floating swimming pools were introduced to the Danish capital's harbor after the city's shipbuilding industry collapsed. These pools turned an unused space into a playground for swimmers, divers, water polo enthusiasts, and boaters, especially on hot summer days . In recent years, cold plunging has also risen in popularity as a way to help with mental and physical health—nowadays, you can expect winter swimming clubs with sauna access along the harbor to have lengthy waiting lists. The new bathing house was designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates and has been 8 years in the making. Rasmus Hjortshøj The next time you visit Copenhagen, there's even more reason to pack a swimsuit . The city’s historic waterfront welcomes a long-awaited new addition on Saturday, December 5: a public swimming pool set to become a new landmark along the city's harbor. Designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates, Kai is the new 62,500 square-foot bathing house that has been eight years in the making. It promises ten pools in total, including an open-air rooftop pool and a heated onsen overlooking Copenhagen Harbor. Delayed due to the pandemic and its knock-on effects, the pool was originally slated to open in 2021 and now joins the list of architecturally distinct buildings lining Copenhagen Harbor, including the modern Opera House and the Royal Danish Playhouse. This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag. By Carla Vianna October 28, 2026 Courtesy Fasano / Daniel Pinheiro Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story “I live where you vacation” takes on a whole other meaning when, like me, you're based in Rio de Janeiro . I live smack in the middle of South America ’s two hottest beaches—Copacabana and Ipanema—but it’s not the ocean that keeps me in Brazil's buzziest city. It’s the life that happens around it. It’s the sound of the first coconuts being cut open on the beach in the early morning, the sight of barefoot surfers passing beneath my window, and the honey-like melody of bossa nova flowing from a nearby beach kiosk. Not everyone can live here, of course. But luckily, the best hotels in Rio de Janeiro give you a good taste of what it feels like to be a local in Brazil’s most exciting metropolis. Over the past six years, I’ve come to appreciate how each neighborhood lets you experience the city differently. Copacabana delivers the high-energy hustle and bustle you’d expect from a place that hosts the biggest Carnival celebration on Earth. In contrast, Leblon offers a quieter, more upscale seaside rhythm. And then there’s Santa Teresa, secluded on the forested hilltops, a tried-and-true bohemian village that’s managed to hold onto its personality despite the city’s rising tourism numbers. The hotels below span these special neighborhoods, with each property offering its own unique take on life in Rio, with Brazilian design, memorable views, and hospitality that’ll make you want to stick around just a little bit longer. Read on for the best hotels in Rio de Janeiro, according to our editors. By Kat Chen October 27, 2026 Unsplash / Jesse Dittmar Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel: The New Miss Marple Mystery by Agatha Christie and Lucy Foley $27 Bookshop.org $30 $21 (30% off) Amazon When we think of Agatha Christie and travel, our minds naturally drift to the nimble Hercule Poirot, especially following Kenneth Branagh’s cinematic revival of the franchise which took the globe-trotting detective from the plush interiors of the Orient Express to a glamorous river steamer on the Nile to a decaying Venetian palazzo . The world of June Marple, the elderly amateur detective Christie featured in a dozen novels and 20 short stories, is considerably quainter. An unassuming spinster settled in the English countryside, the majority of Miss Marple's mysteries have taken place right in her own backyard. But a new novel by Lucy Foley is setting Poirot aside and blowing the dust off the mild-mannered Marple by whisking her away to an extravagant Swiss Alps adventure. The first Miss Marple mystery in 50 years, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel places the incorrigible Victorian gossip in the same shoes as the likes of 007 and Sherlock Holmes as she finds herself at the center of another whodunnit deep in the bowels of The Grand Alpine Hotel, a cozy Swiss ski chalet . With hidden speakeasies, ice-skating waiters, and unforgiving mountainsides, it’s clear Marple is far away from the fictional English hamlet of St. Mary Mead where many of her stories have played out. Condé Nast Traveler spoke with The Guest List author Lucy Foley, who answered the Christie estate's call to pen the latest installment of the Marple franchise, on why she wanted to set this historic new installment abroad, the layered history of the Alps, and what makes Miss Marple such a great traveler. Why transport Miss Marple from the quaint world of St. Mary Mead to the Swiss Alps? The location is where this whole project came to life for me. By Margaret Littman October 27, 2026 Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Music City is rooted in the art of spinning a good yarn. There’s no country music, no Taylor Swift , no late nights chatting at the bar or mornings at breakfast recapping last night without storytelling. And while hotels may once have been merely places to rest your head, today’s best hotels in Nashville are as connected to storytelling as the city where they’re based. There are inns connected to the land and the story of Middle Tennessee; its outdoor adventures and rich soil. There are hotels that explore the city’s history from its role in the suffrage movement to its location on a railway hub to more intimate history about people and places that shaped Nashville. And of course, there’s the hotel that tells the story of Dolly Parton, from the Smoky Mountains to her philanthropic Imagination Library. The beauty of these hotels is that no two are the same, although their stories are interconnected. Each time you come to Nashville and stay at a different hotel, you get a different chapter of the city's full story. These are the best hotels in Nashville for a truly intimate take on the Tennessean capital. items.title: Building a Sustainable Future: Apple's Environmental Commitment | Softer Volumes
items.text: Building a Sustainable Future: Apple's Environmental Commitment | Softer Volumes Building a Sustainable Future: Apple's Environmental Commitment | Softer Volumes Softer Volumes Building a Sustainable Future: Apple’s Environmental Commitment Apple’s latest releases reflect its commitment to the climate Known for its innovative designs and industry-leading technologies, Apple is demonstrating its commitment to more sustainable practices. At last month’s Apple Event there was a noticeable focus on the company’s progress towards its climate goals—the result of ongoing dedicated efforts to reduce the impact of its products across their life cycle. With the unveiling of the iPhone 15 lineup and Apple Watch Series 9 come some significant leaps in sustainability. As always, these new products offer improved performance on previous models, but they also offer dramatically improved environmental specs. The new Apple Watch is the company’s first ever carbon-neutral product; a huge step towards Apple 2030, which will see every Apple product carbon neutral by the end of 2030. Emissions for each model have been reduced by at least 75% through the use of 100% clean energy in production, 30% recycled or renewable materials, and carrying out 50% of shipping without air transportation. Any remaining carbon is offset through high-quality carbon credits. What’s more, Apple has taken this commitment a step further by investing in wind and solar power, which it will use to match 100% of the expected electricity use for charging for each carbon neutral Apple Watch. The new lineup also sees a further reduction in plastic use, with 100% fibre-based packaging. In line with Apple’s goal to use 100% recycled materials in key components by 2025, the new iPhone is built with a higher proportion of recycled materials, such as 100% recycled rare earth minerals and cobalt. With the iPhone 15 also comes the introduction of Grid Forecast in the Home app (available only in the contiguous United States at the time of publishing) that shows users when their grid has access to cleaner energy sources; for example, when an excess of solar or wind power is being produced, or when electricity is being generated with lower emissions. This allows and encourages users to focus their electricity use around these times, potentially lowering their environmental impact. Apple’s accessories haven’t been ignored in these environmental initiatives, either. The company will no longer use leather in any of its product lines. It will instead be replaced with FineWoven, a soft and stylish yet durable twill fabric made from 68% post-consumer recycled content—now available on iPhone MagSafe cases and wallets, and the Magnetic Link and Modern Buckle Apple Watch straps. The Sport Loop Apple Watch strap has also been redesigned and is now constructed with 82% recycled fibre, partially sourced from discarded fishing nets. items.title: A Reimagined Classic and New Designs from Herman Miller | Softer Volumes
items.text: A Reimagined Classic and New Designs from Herman Miller | Softer Volumes A Reimagined Classic and New Designs from Herman Miller | Softer Volumes Softer Volumes A Reimagined Classic and New Designs from Herman Miller A closer look at the brand’s recent collaborations with the Eames Office and Porto-based Singaporean designer Gabriel Tan For over one hundred years, Herman Miller has produced some of the world’s most iconic furniture designs and collaborated with some of the industry’s most influential names, such as Eames Office, George Nelson, and Isami Noguchi. Their most recent releases continue this legacy, simultaneously revitalising classic pieces and embracing contemporary design. The newly renamed Eames Turned Stool reimagines and rejuvenates the classic Eames Walnut Stool. Designed by Charles and Ray Eames in 1960 for the lobbies of the Time & Life Building at the Rockefeller Center in New York, the stool’s sculptural design has become something of an icon. A concave top and bottom not only allow the stool to be used as both a seat and a table, but also to be placed either way up. Thanks to its pleasing geometric forms, it can also serve as a standalone piece, decorative in its own right. Four variations were created for the Time & Life building, three of which became part of Herman Miller’s collection. Now, in celebration of the company’s centenary, the fourth shape, Shape “D”, has been added to the lineup, along with a new ebonised ash finish, available as an alternative to the original turned walnut. Herman Miller have also collaborated with Singaporean designer Gabriel Tan on two new pieces: the Luva Modular Sofa Group and Cyclade Tables . A commitment to craftsmanship, comfort, and versatility underpins the collaboration. Both pieces feature organic shapes and soft curves that invite touch and interaction. Inspired by the firm, padded forms of boxing gloves, the Luva—Portuguese for “glove”—Modular Sofa features a folding back that transforms it from a firm, supportive chair to a more relaxed seat ideal for lounging. Hidden bars allow modules to be combined or separated easily, allowing complete customisation for each user’s space and needs. The Cyclade Tables range—inspired by the form of Pangea and the flowing, fluid sculptures of artist Isami Noguchi—consists of three unique tables which can be nested together or used independently. Together, the tables intertwine and intersect, creating one harmonious piece. Apart, each table is distinct enough to stand alone. The low variation is available with an optional glass bowl that fits into the table’s circular cut-out, perfect for displaying plants or treasured objects. These collaborations are testament to Herman Miller’s enduring spirit of creative endeavour, and their dedication to innovative design and the craft of furniture construction. items.title: Lauriston Road  - Gundry + Ducker
items.text: Lauriston Road - Gundry + Ducker Gundry + Ducker + Projects Studio News Commercial Practice Residential People Public Contact + Projects Studio News Contact Gundry + Ducker IMAGES HERE Lauriston Road Text Location: Hackney London Photography: Andrew Meredith The project is a two-storey extension to a ground floor and basement maisonette within a Victorian terraced house. Previously ,across the rear of the house , was a collection of ramshackle lean-to structures all sitting a metre below the adjacent garden level. The new extension now contains the main living space plus a studio room upstairs. The extension gives the lower flat its own identity, envisaged as a separate building sitting in front of the original, the rear elevation introduces a formal facade in front of the informal original. The ground floor spaceserves as a kitchen, dining and sitting area, and although a simple rectangular space the articulation of the wall materials helps define the different areas of the room. The unlit space at the centre of the plan is used as a bathroom and utility room. A bespoke kitchen is partially pushed into a recess at the back of the room. The kitchen has a concrete worktop and the cupboards are made from black Valchromat a secret door leads to the utility room. A large roof light brings light into the back of the room and sits above the dining table. The room at the upper level is a studio for the client who is a photographer, this has an L shaped corner window giving views across the back gardens. A patio area was excavated to be level with the house with steps leading up to the garden level. July 2018 Filed under Residential

items.title: North Audley Canteen  - Gundry + Ducker
items.text: North Audley Canteen - Gundry + Ducker Gundry + Ducker + Projects Studio News Commercial Practice Residential People Public Contact + Projects Studio News Contact Gundry + Ducker North Audley Canteen Text Location: Mayfair. Photography: Andrew Meredith. We were asked to redesign the basement of NAC (North Audley Cantine) in Mayfair.(formerly a bar). It is a popular hangout for Bond-Street shoppers and the after-work crowd to enjoy French-style shared plates, desserts and bespoke cocktails. We were interested in 1940’s Hollywood for its combination of optimism and glamor, a deliberate contrast to the rough wood/industrial aesthetic still common place in London. We used rounded shapes, rich-blue velvet seating booths, light marble table tops, see-through partitions, mirrors and bespoke light fitting to create a contrast for the floor above and to bring a sense of space and light to a windowless space. November 2017 Filed under commercial

items.title: White Rabbit House  - Gundry + Ducker
items.text: White Rabbit House - Gundry + Ducker Gundry + Ducker + Projects Studio News Commercial Practice Residential People Public Contact + Projects Studio News Contact Gundry + Ducker {image 35 IMAGES HERE White Rabbit House Text LOCATION : Islington London PHOTOGRAPHY : Andrew Meredith History The house is part of a terrace of 1970s neo-Georgian houses, built on the site of demolished large Victorian Villas. This terrace is one of many similar examples built in a ten year period from the mid 1960s around Canonbury. The first of these ,a terrace built in Canonbury Place was designed by Raymond Erith one of the leading classical Architects of the period. This later terrace, however, was by a unnamed house builders architect. The Design Whilst the front facade was designed in the Neo-Georgian style, the interior layout and design were generic 1970’s house builder. Stripping out the entire interior back to just the external walls and the roof, we inserted a new interior as a modern interpretation of a Georgian house interior. The design is centred around a cantilevered pill shaped staircase that sits in a triple height space with the upper rooms accessed directly off the stair. The hallway has a chequer board floor in marble and terrazzo with the terrazzo continuing up the staircase. A rear extension provides a kitchen and dining space. A full width roof light illuminates the middle of the plan. Local planning restrictions inexplicably prevented dormer windows to the rear (or any form of roof extension). Our solution was to move the floor levels around to achieve three stories, within the available space. The design was intended to provide a contrasting route through the house. The initial volume of the entrance hall is contrasted by the scale of the arched tunnel beyond. There is a visual link through the house from the front door through to the arched garden window and the space beyond. The rear facade is composed of white brick and terrazzo and alludes to Georgian marble fireplace surrounds. The project was an opportunity to explore the skills of craftsman some of whom we have been working with for some years. The cantilevered staircase was built entirely on site and although contemporary is built in the same way a Victorian or Georgian staircase would be built. We also worked with a terrazzo specialist on a bespoke mix terrazzo used both in-situ and precast formats. This formed the stairtreads, the flooring, work tops and the cladding of the rear façade. Update we have added some interior shots with the furniture and shots of the complete garden. October 2019 Filed under Residential

items.title: Holm  - Gundry + Ducker
items.text: Holm - Gundry + Ducker Gundry + Ducker + Projects Studio News Commercial Practice Residential People Public Contact + Projects Studio News Contact Gundry + Ducker IMAGES HERE Holm Text LOCATION : South Petherton Somerset PHOTOGRAPHY Holm is a restaurant within a converted Hamstone bank in South Petherton, Somerset. The bank, originally a house, had been significantly altered over the years. The principal rooms and staircase had been lost, and significant further alteration would be required to accommodate its new use. The challenge became how to convert the building without losing the remaining character. The strategy, in the end, was to focus on materiality, both the building existing fabric and our interventions. We exposed specific parts of the fabric of the building by cutting away plaster and cutting openings, adding a simple pallet of ground concrete, solid oak and white render. March 2022 Filed under Commercial

items.title: ReCasting by Alison Brooks Architects. an installation at the Venice Bienalle.  - Luke Hayes Photography
items.text: ReCasting by Alison Brooks Architects. an installation at the Venice Bienalle. - Luke Hayes Photography Canada Water recasting photography film contact tear sheet Alison Brooks Architects were invited by the 16th International Architecture Exhibition curators Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara of Grafton Architects to respond to this year’s theme of ‘Freespace’ by addressing the subject of housing and urban dwelling. We have created a large-scale, site specific installation that simulates the critical freespaces of their work in housing as four inhabitable ‘totems’: Threshold, Inhabited Edge, Passage, and Roofspace. The totems invite exploration, emerging from a unifying plinth to frame an amphitheatre and collective gathering space. Each totem offers a particular spatial, emotional and sensory experience, harnessing the Corderie’s specific qualities of light and volume. It has been this practice’s mission to reveal housing architecture’s civic role and its potential for meaningful, subjective experience. items.title: Pyeongchang pavilion 2018  - Luke Hayes Photography
items.text: Pyeongchang pavilion 2018 - Luke Hayes Photography Canada Water recasting photography film contact tear sheet The Darkest building on earth.. This structure was designed by Asif Khan architects for Hyundai. It was they're pavilion at the 2018 Winter Olympics in South Korea. The building was coated VBX 2 which absorbs 99% of light. It was by far the coldest environment I have ever worked in, with the daytime temperature hovering around -11. The air was extremely dry and with almost no wind it made it bearable to be outside for a period of time. Shooting this pavilion was a really interesting challenge, as I wasn't looking for details or structural elements, rather capturing the darkness and the feeling of looking in to the void. It was very interesting to move around the project and capture it with some of the local surroundings framing it. especially the contrast of the hazy blue mountains in the background and the extreme black of the pavilion. items.title: Letting Go — Suellen Parker
items.text: Letting Go — Suellen Parker Artwork Stacey Abrams - Lift One, You Lift All something new About My Process About Contact Suellen Parker Artwork Stacey Abrams - Lift One, You Lift All something new About My Process About Contact Letting Go This work investigates how one can find one’s voice in this over stimulating world full of standards and ideas that tell us the right way to be. In my previous body of work, Incurable Perfection , the characters look to culture for guidance on how to create themselves. In Letting Go , the characters look within themselves for the answers of who they are, letting go of cultural standards and expectations. By taking a break from the chaos of daily life, they are able to connect with themselves through stillness and play; two ways to listen and discover one’s authentic self. The hope is that within these moments, the characters will let go of their expectations of how they should be, allowing space for their behaviors and appearances to reflect who they are.
